title: EXPOSÉ XXVI PARABOLIC SUBGROUPS OF REDUCTIVE GROUPS

pages.title: EXPOSÉ XXVI PARABOLIC SUBGROUPS OF REDUCTIVE GROUPS

blocks.html:
EXPOSÉ XXVI
PARABOLIC SUBGROUPS OF REDUCTIVE GROUPSby M. Demazure

This exposé studies the parabolic subgroups of reductive groups. Its essential result is the conjugacy theorem (5.14). The essential tool is the notion of transversal position of two parabolic subgroups, a notion which is studied systematically in no 4. Another fact plays an important role: the decomposition of the unipotent radical of a parabolic subgroup into successive extensions of vector groups (2.1).
Various schemes associated with a reductive group are studied in no 3; no 6 deals with the trivial subtori of a reductive group and with their relations with parabolic subgroups.

Finally, in no 7, we briefly explain how one formulates, over a semi-local base, the "relative theory" of reductive groups as it is set out in the case of fields in the article of A. BOREL and J. TITS, Groupes Réductifs, Publications Mathématiques de l'IHÉS, no 27. In that article, cited [BT] in what follows, the reader will moreover find, in the case of a base field, further results which have not been touched upon here.
1. Reminders. Levi subgroups

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) a sub-\(S\)-prescheme in groups of \(G\). One says that \(P\) is a parabolic subgroup of \(G\) if

(i) \(P\) is smooth over \(S\),

(ii) for each \(s \in S\), the quotient \(\overline{s}\)-prescheme \(G_{\overline{s}}/P_{\overline{s}}\) is proper (i.e. BIBLE, 6-09, th. 4, \(P_{\overline{s}}\) contains a Borel group of \(G_{\overline{s}}\)).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.2 (Exp. XXII, 5.8.5)

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\). Then \(P\) is closed in \(G\), with connected fibres, and one has \[ P = \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(P). \] Moreover, the quotient sheaf \(G/P\) is representable by an \(S\)-prescheme smooth and projective over \(S\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.3 (Exp. XXII, 5.3.9 et 5.3.11)

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) and \(P'\) two parabolic subgroups of \(G\). The following conditions are equivalent:

(i) \(P\) and \(P'\) are conjugate in \(G\), locally for the étale (resp. (fpqc)) topology.

(ii) For each \(s \in S\), \(P_{\overline{s}}\) and \(P'_{\overline{s}}\) are conjugate by an element of \(G(\overline{s})\).

(iii) The strict transporter \(\underline{\mathrm{Transt}}_G(P, P')\) of \(P\) into \(P'\) \[ (\underline{\mathrm{Transt}}_G(P, P')(S') = \{ g \in G(S'),\ \mathrm{int}(g)P_{S'} = P'_{S'} \}) \] is a closed subprescheme of \(G\), smooth and of finite presentation over \(S\), which is a principal homogeneous bundle under \(P\) (on the right) and under \(P'\) (on the left).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.4

Let \(S\) be a non-empty prescheme, \((G, T, M, R)\) a split reductive \(S\)-group, \(R'\) a subset of \(R\). The following conditions on \(R'\) are equivalent:

(i) \(\mathfrak{g}_{R'} = \mathfrak{t} \oplus \coprod_{\alpha \in R'} \mathfrak{g}^\alpha\) is the Lie Algebra of a parabolic subgroup of \(G\) containing \(T\) (necessarily unique, Exp. XXII, 5.3.5).

(ii) \(R'\) is of type (R) (Exp. XXII, 5.4.2) and contains a system of positive roots.

(iii) \(R'\) is a closed subset of \(R\) and \(\alpha \in R,\ -\alpha \notin R' \Longrightarrow \alpha \in R'\).

(iv) There exist a system of simple roots \(R_0\), and a subset \(A\) of \(R_0\) such that \(R'\) is the union of the set of positive roots and of the set of negative roots which are linear combinations of the elements of \(A\).

(v) \(R'\) contains a system of simple roots of \(R\); moreover, if \(R_0 \subset R'\) is a system of simple roots of \(R\) and if one puts \[ A = (-R') \cap R_0, \] \(R'\) is the union of the set of positive roots and of the set of negative roots which are linear combinations of the elements of \(A\).

One has (i) \(\Leftrightarrow\) (ii) by Exp. XXII, 5.4.5 (ii). One has (iii) \(\Rightarrow\) (ii) by Exp. XXI, 3.3.6 and Exp. XXII, 5.4.7. One evidently has (v) \(\Rightarrow\) (iv) \(\Rightarrow\) (iii). One has (iii) \(\Rightarrow\) (v) by Exp. XXI, 3.3.6 and 3.3.10.

It therefore remains to prove that (i) implies that \(R'\) is a closed subset of \(R\). Now this last assertion may be checked on an arbitrary geometric fibre; one may therefore suppose that \(S\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field.

Let \(P\) be the parabolic group of \(G\) containing \(T\) whose Lie algebra is \(\mathfrak{g}_{R'}\). Since the Borel groups of \(P\) are the Borel groups of \(G\) contained in \(P\), it follows from BIBLE, 12-07, th. 1, and from Exp. XXII, 5.4.5 (i), that if one denotes by \(U\) the unipotent radical of \(P\), \(T \cdot U\) is the subgroup of \(G\) containing \(T\) with Lie algebra \[ \mathfrak{g}_{R''} = \mathfrak{t} \oplus \coprod_{\alpha \in R''} \mathfrak{g}^\alpha, \] where \(R''\) is the intersection of the systems of positive roots of \(R\) contained in \(R'\). It follows in particular that \(R''\) is closed and that \(R'' \cap (-R'') = \emptyset\). On the other hand, the group \(H = P/U\) is reductive, the canonical image \(\overline{T}\) of \(T\) is a maximal torus of it (\(T \to \overline{T}\) is an isomorphism), and one has an isomorphism of \(T\)-Modules, i.e. of graded vector spaces of type \(M\) \[ \mathrm{Lie}(H) \simeq \mathfrak{t} \oplus \coprod_{\alpha \in R_s} \mathfrak{g}^\alpha, \] where \(R_s\) is the complement of \(R''\) in \(R'\). It follows that \(R_s\) is naturally identified with the set of roots of \(H\) relative to \(\overline{T}\), and in particular satisfies \(R_s = -R_s\). It follows at once that one has \[ R'' = \{\alpha \in R',\ -\alpha \notin R'\}, \qquad R_s = \{\alpha \in R',\ -\alpha \in R'\}. \]

Let us now show that \(R'\) is closed. Let \(\alpha, eta \in R'\), \(\alpha + eta \in R\); let us prove that \(\alpha + eta \in R'\). If \(\alpha, eta \in R''\), then \(\alpha + eta \in R''\) since \(R''\) is closed. If \(\alpha \in R_s\), \( eta \in R''\), and if \(\alpha + eta otin R'\), then \(\alpha + eta \in -R''\), and one has \(-\alpha = s + (-(\alpha + eta)) \in R''\) since \(R''\) is closed, which implies \(-\alpha \in R'\), hence \(-\alpha \in R_s\), and contradicts the fact that \(R_s \cap R'' = \emptyset\). It therefore remains to study the case where \(\alpha, eta \in R_s\). If \(\alpha + eta otin R'\), then \(\alpha + eta \in -R''\). But, since \(\alpha + eta eq 0\), there exists a system of positive roots of the root system \(R_s\) containing \(\alpha\) and \(s\), hence a Borel group of \(H = P/U\) containing the canonical image of \(U_\alpha\) and \(U_ eta\). Its inverse image in \(P\) is a Borel group containing \(U_\alpha\), \(U_ eta\) and \(U\), hence \(U_\alpha\), \(U_ eta\) and \(U_{-(\alpha+ eta)}\), which is impossible.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.5

A parabolic subgroup of a reductive group is of type (RC) (Exp. XXII, 5.11.1).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.6 (Exp. XXII, 5.11.4)

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\).

(i) \(P\) possesses a largest invariant subprescheme in groups, smooth and of finite presentation over \(S\), with connected and unipotent geometric fibres. It is a characteristic subgroup of \(P\), called the unipotent radical of \(P\), denoted \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P)\). The quotient sheaf \(P/\mathrm{rad}^u(P)\) is representable by a reductive \(S\)-group.

(ii) If \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(P\), \(P\) possesses a reductive subgroup \(L\) containing \(T\), such that:

(a) Every reductive subgroup of \(P\) containing \(T\) is contained in \(L\).

(b) \(P\) is the semi-direct product \(L \cdot \mathrm{rad}^u(P)\), i.e. the canonical morphism \(L \to P/\mathrm{rad}^u(P)\) is an isomorphism.

Moreover, \(L\) is the unique subgroup (resp. reductive subgroup) of \(P\), containing \(T\) and satisfying (b) (resp. (a)). Finally, one has \[ \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_P(L) = L, \qquad \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_P(T) = \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_L(T). \]

A subgroup \(L\) of \(P\) satisfying condition (b) above is called a Levi subgroup of \(P\). It is a maximal reductive subgroup of \(P\); indeed, it is reductive, being isomorphic to \(P/\mathrm{rad}^u(P)\); let us show that it is maximal for this property; let \(L'\) be a reductive subgroup of \(P\) containing \(L\); to prove that \(L' = L\), one may argue locally for the (fpqc) topology, and hence suppose that \(L\) possesses a maximal torus \(T\), and one is reduced to 1.6 (ii).

If \(L\) and \(L'\) are two Levi subgroups of \(P\), then \(L\) and \(L'\) are conjugate in \(P\), locally for the (fpqc) topology. Indeed, locally for this topology, one may suppose that \(L\) (resp. \(L'\)) possesses a maximal torus \(T\) (resp. \(T'\)); since \(T\) and \(T'\) are conjugate in \(P\) locally for the (fpqc) topology, one may suppose \(T = T'\), and one then has \(L = L'\), by 1.6 (ii). But since \(P = L \cdot \mathrm{rad}^u(P)\) and \(\underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_P(L) = L\), one deduces at once:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.8

If \(L\) and \(L'\) are two Levi subgroups of the parabolic subgroup \(G\) of the reductive group \(G\), there exists a unique \(u \in \mathrm{rad}^u(P)(S)\) such that \(\mathrm{int}(u)L = L'\).

Let us denote by \(\underline{\mathrm{Lev}}(P)\) the functor of Levi subgroups of \(P\): for \(S' \to S\), \(\underline{\mathrm{Lev}}(P)(S')\) is the set of Levi subgroups of \(P_{S'}\). From 1.8 one deduces:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.9

Let \(P\) be a parabolic subgroup of the reductive \(S\)-group \(G\). Then \(\underline{\mathrm{Lev}}(P)\) is a principal homogeneous bundle under the \(S\)-group \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P)\), and in particular is representable by an \(S\)-prescheme smooth and affine over \(S\), with integral geometric fibres.
It follows immediately from 1.6:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.10

Let \(P\) be a parabolic subgroup of the reductive \(S\)-group \(G\). The functor \(\underline{\mathrm{Tor}}(P)\) of maximal tori of \(P\) is representable by a smooth affine \(S\)-prescheme, the "relation \(L \supset T\)" defines a morphism \[ \underline{\mathrm{Tor}}(P) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Lev}}(P), \] the fibre of this morphism over \(L \in \underline{\mathrm{Lev}}(P)(S)\) is identified with \(\underline{\mathrm{Tor}}(L)\) (Exp. XXII, 5.8.3).
The first assertion of 1.10 is a consequence of the two others and of Exp. XXII, 5.8.3.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.11

Let \(S\) be a non-empty prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\), \(\mathscr{E} = (T, M, R, R_0, (X_\alpha)_{\alpha \in R_0})\) a pinning of \(G\). One says that \(\mathscr{E}\) is adapted to \(P\), or that \(\mathscr{E}\) is a pinning of the pair \((G, P)\) if \(P \supset T\) and if the Lie Algebra of \(P\) is of the form \(\mathfrak{t} \oplus \coprod_{\alpha \in R'} \mathfrak{g}^\alpha\), where \(R'\) is a subset of \(R\) containing \(R_0\).
In particular, if \(T \subset B\) is the Killing couple defined by the pinning, one has \(T \subset B \subset P\).

Under the preceding conditions, one writes \(R_0(P) = R_0 \cap (-R')\). One has \((\alpha \in R_0(P)) \Leftrightarrow (\alpha \in R_0\) and \(U_{-\alpha} \subset P) \Leftrightarrow (\alpha \in R_0\) and \(U_{-\alpha} \cap P \neq e)\), by Exp. XXII, 5.4.3.
It follows at once from 1.4 (v) and Exp. XXII, 5.11.3:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.12

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\), \((T, M, R_0, (X_\alpha)_{\alpha \in R_0})\) a pinning of \(\mathscr{E}\) adapted to \(P\), \(R_0(P)\) the subset of \(R_0\) defined above.

(i) The unipotent radical \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P)\) of \(P\) is none other than \[ U_{R''} = \prod_{\alpha \in R''} U_\alpha, \] where \(R''\) is the set of positive roots which in their decomposition over \(R_0\) contain at least one element of \(R_0(P)\) with a non-zero coefficient.

(ii) The unique Levi subgroup \(L\) of \(P\) containing \(T\) is none other than \[ Z_{R_0(P)} = \underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(T_{R_0(P)}), \] where \(T_{R_0(P)}\) is the maximal torus of the common kernel of the \(\alpha \in R_0(P)\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.13

Every Levi subgroup \(L\) of the parabolic subgroup \(P\) of the reductive group \(G\) is a critical subgroup of \(G\), i.e. satisfies (Exp. XXII, 5.10.4): \[ L = \underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(\mathrm{rad}(L)). \]
This follows at once from 1.12, Exp. XXII, 5.10.6, and from the following lemma, contained in 1.4 and Exp. XXII, 5.4.1:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.14

Locally for the étale topology, every pair \((G, P)\), where \(P\) is a parabolic subgroup of the reductive group \(G\), can be pinned (1.11).
Let us note:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.15

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\), \(\mathscr{E}\) and \(\mathscr{E}'\) two pinnings of \(G\) adapted to \(P\). The unique inner automorphism of \(G\) over \(S\) which transforms \(\mathscr{E}\) into \(\mathscr{E}'\) (Exp. XXIV, 1.5) comes from \(P\), by the morphism \[ P \longrightarrow P/\underline{\mathrm{Centr}}(P) = P/\underline{\mathrm{Centr}}(G) \longrightarrow G/\underline{\mathrm{Centr}}(G). \]
Indeed, it suffices to argue as in Exp. XXIV, 1.5, using:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.16 (Exp. XXII, 5.3.14 et 5.2.6)

The maximal tori (resp. Borel groups, resp. Killing couples) of a parabolic subgroup \(P\) of the reductive \(S\)-group \(G\) are conjugate in \(P\), locally for the étale topology.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.17

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) and \(P'\) two parabolic subgroups of \(G\), \(B\) a Borel group contained in \(P\) and \(P'\). If \(P\) and \(P'\) are conjugate in \(G\), locally for the étale topology, then \(P = P'\).

Indeed, one may suppose that there exists \(g \in G(S)\) such that \(\mathrm{int}(g)P = P'\). Then \(B\) and \(\mathrm{int}(g)^{-1}B\) are two Borel groups of \(P\). After possibly extending \(S\), one may by 1.16 suppose that there exists \(p \in P(S)\) with \(\mathrm{int}(p)\,\mathrm{int}(g^{-1})B = B\). Then \[ p\, g^{-1} \in \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(B)(S) = B(S), \] and \(g \in B(S) \cdot p \subset P(S)\), hence \(P' = \mathrm{int}(g)P = P\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 1.18

If \(P\) and \(P'\) are two parabolic subgroups of \(G\) containing one and the same Borel group, then \(P \cap P'\) is again a parabolic subgroup of \(G\). Indeed, it is smooth along the unit section (Exp. XXII, 5.4.5), and it contains a Borel group.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.19

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(G'\) its derived group (Exp. XXII, 6.2.1).

(i) The maps \[ P \mapsto P' = P \cap G' \qquad \text{and} \qquad P \mapsto P' \cdot \mathrm{rad}(G) = \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(P') \] are mutually inverse bijections between the set of parabolic subgroups of \(G\) and the set of parabolic subgroups of \(G'\). One has \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P) = \mathrm{rad}^u(P')\).

(ii) Let \(P\) be a parabolic subgroup of \(G\) and \(P' = P \cap G'\). The maps \[ L \mapsto L' = L \cap G' = L \cap P' \] \[ L' \mapsto L' \cdot \mathrm{rad}(G) = \underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(\mathrm{rad}(L')) \] are mutually inverse bijections between the set of Levi subgroups of \(P\) and the set of Levi subgroups of \(P'\). Moreover, one has \(\mathrm{rad}(L') = (\mathrm{rad}(L) \cap G')^0\).
The proof (by reduction to the split case, for example) is carried out without difficulty and is left to the reader, as is that, immediate, of:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.20

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\), \(L\) a Levi subgroup of \(P\). The maps \[ Q \mapsto Q \cap L = Q', \qquad Q' \mapsto Q' \cdot \mathrm{rad}^u(P) \] are mutually inverse bijections between the set of parabolic subgroups of \(G\) contained in \(P\) and the set of parabolic subgroups of \(L\). Moreover, the Levi subgroups of \(Q'\) are the Levi subgroups of \(Q\) contained in \(L\).
One may complete 1.6 in the following manner:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.21

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\).

(i) \(P\) possesses a largest invariant subgroup, smooth and of finite presentation over \(S\), with connected and solvable geometric fibres. It is a characteristic subgroup of \(P\), called the radical of \(P\), and denoted \(\mathrm{rad}(P)\). The quotient sheaf \(P/\mathrm{rad}(P)\) is representable by a semi-simple \(S\)-group.

(ii) If \(L\) is a Levi subgroup of \(P\), \(\mathrm{rad}(P)\) is the semi-direct product of \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P)\) and \(\mathrm{rad}(L)\); one has \(\mathrm{rad}(L) = L \cap \mathrm{rad}(P)\), hence \(L = \underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(L \cap \mathrm{rad}(P))\), and \(P/\mathrm{rad}(P) \simeq L/\mathrm{rad}(L)\).

Indeed, assertion (i) being local, one may suppose that \(G\) possesses a Levi subgroup \(L\), and one is reduced to proving that \(R = \mathrm{rad}^u(P) \cdot \mathrm{rad}(L)\) possesses the properties announced in (i), which is immediate. For (ii), it only remains to prove that \(\mathrm{rad}(L) = L \cap \mathrm{rad}(P)\), which follows at once from the fact that \(L \cap \mathrm{rad}(P)\) is smooth and with connected fibres, \(L\) being the centralizer of a torus.

pages.title: 2. Structure of the unipotent radical of a parabolic subgroup

blocks.html: 2. Structure of the unipotent radical of a parabolic subgroup

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\), \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P)\) its unipotent radical. There exists a sequence of subpreschemes in groups of \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P)\) \[ \mathrm{rad}^u(P) = U_0 \supset U_1 \supset U_2 \supset \cdots \supset U_n \supset \cdots \] possessing the following properties:

(i) Each \(U_i\) is smooth, with connected fibres, characteristic and closed in \(P\). The commutator of a section of \(U_i\) and a section of \(U_j\) is a section of \(U_{i+j+1}\) (over a variable \(S' \to S\)).

(ii) For each \(i \geqslant 0\), there exist a locally free \(\mathscr{O}_S\)-Module \(\mathscr{E}_i\) and an isomorphism of \(S\)-sheaves in groups \[ U_i/U_{i+1} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathbf{W}(\mathscr{E}_i). \] Moreover, the automorphisms of \(P\) (over a variable \(S' \to S\)) operate linearly on \(\mathbf{W}(\mathscr{E}_i)\).

(iii) For every \(s \in S\), one has \(U_{n,\,s} = e\) for \(n > \dim(\mathrm{rad}^u(P)_s)\).

Let us first suppose the pair \((G, P)\) pinnable. Let \((T, M, R, R_0, \ldots)\) be a pinning of \(G\) adapted to \(P\); let \(R_0(P)\) be the subset of \(R_0\) defined by \(P\). Let \(\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_p\) be the elements of \(R_0(P)\), \(\beta_1, \ldots, \beta_q\) the elements of \(R_0 - R_0(P)\). Every root \(\gamma \in R\) is written in a unique way \[ \gamma = a_1\alpha_1 + \cdots + a_p\alpha_p + b_1\beta_1 + \cdots + b_q\beta_q. \] Let us put \[ a(\gamma) = a_1 + \cdots + a_p. \] The following properties follow at once from the definitions (cf. 1.12):
(i) \(U_\gamma \subset P \Leftrightarrow a(\gamma) \geqslant 0\).
(ii) \(U_\gamma \subset \mathrm{rad}^u(P) \Leftrightarrow a(\gamma) > 0\).
(iii) \(a(n\gamma + m\gamma') = n\, a(\gamma) + m\, a(\gamma') \qquad n, m \in \mathbf{Z}\).

Let \(R_i\) be the set of roots \(\gamma \in R\) such that \(a(\gamma) > i\). Each \(R_i\) is a closed set of roots satisfying \(R_i \cap (-R_i) = \emptyset\). Let us consider (Exp. XXII, 5.6.5) the \(S\)-group \[ U_i = U_{R_i} = \prod_{\gamma \in R_i} U_\gamma. \] It is a closed subprescheme in groups of \(G\), smooth over \(S\), with connected fibres.

Let \(\alpha, \beta \in R\); let us consider the commutation relation of Exp. XXII, 5.5.2 \[ p_\alpha(x)p_\beta(y)p_\alpha(-x) = p_\beta(y) \prod_{\substack{n, m \in \mathbf{N} \\ n, m \neq 0}} p_{n\alpha+m\beta}(C_{n,m,\alpha,\beta}\, x^n y^m), \] where each \(p_\gamma\) is an isomorphism of vector groups \(\mathbf{G}_{a,\,S} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } U_\gamma\). Let us remark first that if \(a(\alpha) > i\) and \(a(\beta) > j\), one has \[ a(n\alpha + m\beta) = n\, a(\alpha) + m\, a(\beta) \geqslant n(i+1) + m(j+1) > i + j + 1 \] if \(n\) and \(m\) are \(> 0\). It follows that the commutator of a section of \(U_\alpha\) and a section of \(U_\beta\) is a section of \(U_{i+j+1}\) (over a variable \(S' \to S\)), which indeed implies \((U_i, U_j) \subset U_{i+j+1}\). For each \(i \geqslant 0\), the quotient \(U_i/U_{i+1}\) is therefore commutative; it is naturally identified with \[ U_i/U_{i+1} \simeq \prod_{a(\gamma) = i+1} U_\gamma \simeq \mathbf{W}(\mathscr{E}_i), \] where \(\mathscr{E}_i\) is the direct sum of the \(\mathfrak{g}^\gamma\) for \(a(\gamma) = i + 1\).
Let us now return to the commutation formula above, and suppose \(a(\alpha) \geqslant 0\), \(a(\beta) > i\). If \(n, m \in \mathbf{N}\), \(n, m \neq 0\),
– either \(a(n\alpha + m\beta) > i + 1\)
– or \(a(n\alpha + m\beta) = i + 1\), in which case one necessarily has \(m = 1\).

This proves first that \(\mathrm{int}(p_\alpha(x))\) respects \(U_i\) (hence also \(U_{i+1}\)), then that in the expression of \(\mathrm{int}(p_\alpha(x))p_\beta(y)\) there occur, modulo \(U_{i+1}\), only terms of the form \(p_{n\alpha+\beta}(C_{n,1,\alpha,\beta}\, x^n y)\) which are therefore linear in \(y\). It follows that the inner automorphisms of \(U_\alpha\) operate linearly in the quotient \(U_i/U_{i+1}\) identified with \(\mathbf{W}(\mathscr{E}_i)\). Since this is likewise trivially true for the inner automorphisms defined by sections of \(T\), and since \(P\) is generated by \(T\) and the \(U_\alpha\), \(a(\alpha) \geqslant 0\), one deduces:
(i) that each \(U_i\) is invariant in \(P\),
(ii) that the inner automorphisms defined by sections of \(P\) operate linearly in \(U_i/U_{i+1} \simeq \mathbf{W}(\mathscr{E}_i)\).

Let now \((T', M', R', R'_0, \ldots)\) be a new pinning of \(G\) adapted to \(P\). By 1.15, there exists an inner automorphism of \(G\) coming from \(P\) which transforms the old pinning into the new one. After possibly extending \(S\), one may suppose that this inner automorphism is of the form \(\mathrm{int}(p)\), \(p \in P(S)\). If one takes up the preceding constructions by means of the new pinning, it is clear that the groups \(U'_i\) and the isomorphisms \(U'_i/U'_{i+1} \simeq \mathbf{W}(\mathscr{E}'_i)\) obtained are deduced from \(U_i\) and \(U_i/U_{i+1} \simeq \mathbf{W}(\mathscr{E}_i)\) by transport of structure by means of \(\mathrm{int}(p)\). It follows from remarks (i) and (ii) above that one will therefore have \(U'_i = U_i\), and that the two vector structures constructed on \(U_i/U_{i+1} = U'_i/U'_{i+1}\) coincide.

This shows us that the groups \(U_i\) and the vector structures on the quotients \(U_i/U_{i+1}\) are independent of the pinning considered (and in particular invariant under every automorphism of \(P\), as one sees easily).

We have therefore proved the proposition when the pair \((G, P)\) is pinnable (part (iii) is trivial, for the set of orders of the elements of \(R\) is an interval of \(\mathbf{Z}\), so that one can have \(\dim(U_{i,\,s}) = \dim(U_{i+1,\,s})\) only if \(U_{i,\,s} = e\)).

In the general case, there exists a covering family for the (fpqc) topology, \(\{S_j \to S\}\), such that each pair \((G_{S_j}, P_{S_j})\) is pinnable (1.14). By what precedes, one has descent data on the \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P_{S_j})_i\), compatible with the vector structures of the quotients, and one concludes by descent of closed subpreschemes (resp. of locally free Modules).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.2

Let \(S\) be an affine scheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) a parabolic group of \(G\). One has \[ \mathrm{H}^1(S, \mathrm{rad}^u(P)) = 0, \] i.e. every principal homogeneous bundle under \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P)\) is trivial.

Indeed, \(S\) decomposes into a sum of subpreschemes over each of which \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P)\) is of constant relative dimension. One may therefore by (iii) suppose that there exists an \(n\) such that \(U_n = e\). Since \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, U_i/U_{i+1}) = \mathrm{H}^1(S, \mathbf{W}(\mathscr{E}_i)) = 0\) by TDTE I, B, 1.1 (or SGA 1, XI 5.1), one concludes at once.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.3

Under the preceding conditions, \(P\) possesses a Levi subgroup \(L\). If \(L\) is a Levi subgroup of \(P\), the canonical map \[ \mathrm{H}^1(S, L) \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}^1(S, P) \] is bijective (cf. the introduction of Exp. XXIV for the definition of \(\mathrm{H}^1(S,\ )\)).

The first assertion follows from 2.2 and 1.9. The canonical map \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, L) \to \mathrm{H}^1(S, P)\) is surjective, since \(P\) is the semi-direct product \(L \cdot \mathrm{rad}^u(P)\). To prove that it is injective, it suffices to see that for every principal homogeneous bundle \(Q\) under \(L\), one has \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, \mathrm{rad}^u(P)_Q) = 0\), where the index \(Q\) denotes the operation of twisting by the \(L\)-bundle \(Q\). This can be proved in two ways: one may take up again the proof of 2.2, using the fact that the vector structures on the \(U_i/U_{i+1}\) are invariant under \(L\); one may also remark that \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P)_Q\) is identified with the unipotent radical of the parabolic subgroup \(P_Q\) of \(G_Q\), and apply 2.2 to \(P_Q\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.4

Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\). There exists a maximal torus \(T\) of \(G\) contained in \(P\).
Indeed, in view of 2.3, \(P\) possesses a Levi subgroup \(L\), and it suffices to prove that \(L\) possesses a maximal torus, which follows from Exp. XIV, 3.20.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.5

Let \(S\) be an affine scheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\). There exists a locally free \(\mathscr{O}_S\)-Module \(\mathscr{E}\) such that \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P)\) is isomorphic as an \(S\)-scheme to \(\mathbf{W}(\mathscr{E})\).

Indeed, let us prove by induction on \(i\) that one has an isomorphism of \(S\)-preschemes \[ \mathrm{rad}^u(P)/U_i \simeq \mathbf{W}(\mathscr{E}_0 \oplus \mathscr{E}_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathscr{E}_{i-1}). \] This is clear for \(i = 0\). Suppose \(i > 0\); then \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P)/U_i\) is a principal homogeneous bundle with base \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P)/U_{i-1}\), under the group \[ (U_{i-1}/U_i)_{\mathrm{rad}^u(P)/U_{i-1}} \simeq \mathbf{W}(\mathscr{E}_{i-1} \otimes \mathscr{O}_{\mathrm{rad}^u(P)/U_{i-1}}). \] Now the base is affine (for example by the induction hypothesis), hence this bundle is trivial (TDTE or SGA 1 XI, loc. cit.), and there exists an isomorphism of \(S\)-preschemes \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P)/U_i \simeq (\mathrm{rad}^u(P)/U_{i-1}) \times_S (U_{i-1}/U_i)\), which completes the proof.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.6

Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme, \(\{s_i\}\) the set of its closed points, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\). The canonical map \[ \mathrm{rad}^u(P)(S) \longrightarrow \prod_i \mathrm{rad}^u(P)(\mathrm{Spec}\, k(s_i)) \] is surjective.

Indeed, if \(S = \mathrm{Spec}(\mathrm{A})\), \(k(s_i) = \mathrm{A}/\mathfrak{p}_i\), and if \(\mathscr{E}\) is given by the projective (hence flat) module \(E\), we must prove that the map \[ E \longrightarrow \prod_i E \otimes_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{A}/\mathfrak{p}_i \] is surjective. It suffices to do so when \(E = \mathrm{A}\), in which case it is well known (cf. Bourbaki, Alg. Comm. Chap. II, § 1, no 2, proposition 5).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.7

Let \(k\) be an infinite field, \(G\) a reductive \(k\)-group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\); then \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P)(k)\) is dense in \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P)\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.8

Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme, \(\{s_i\}\) the set of its closed points, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\), \(L_i\) a Levi subgroup of \(P_{s_i}\) for each \(i\). There exists a Levi subgroup \(L\) of \(P\) inducing \(L_i\) for each \(i\).

Let indeed \(L_0\) be a Levi subgroup of \(P\) (2.3). Let, for each \(i\), \(u_i \in \mathrm{rad}^u(P)(\mathrm{Spec}(k(s_i)))\) be such that \(\mathrm{int}(u_i)L_{0,\,s_i} = L_i\) (1.8); if \(u \in \mathrm{rad}^u(P)(S)\) induces \(u_i\) for each \(i\) (2.6), then \(L = \mathrm{int}(u)L_0\) answers the question.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.9

In the situation of 2.1, let moreover \(H\) be a subprescheme in groups of \(G\), smooth and of finite presentation over \(S\), with connected fibres, such that \(P \cap H\) contains, locally for the (fpqc) topology, a maximal torus of \(G\). Then for each \(i \geqslant 0\), there exists a locally direct summand sub-Module \(\mathscr{F}_i\) of \(\mathscr{E}_i\) such that the isomorphism \(U_i/U_{i+1} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathbf{W}(\mathscr{E}_i)\) induces an isomorphism of groups \[ (U_i \cap H)/(U_{i+1} \cap H) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathbf{W}(\mathscr{F}_i). \]

Indeed, \(H\) is a subgroup of type (R) of \(G\) (Exp. XXII, 5.2.1). On the other hand, the assertion to be proved is local for the (fpqc) topology, and one may suppose \(G\) split relative to a maximal torus of \(P \cap H\); one may even reduce to the situation of 2.1.1, \(H\) being defined by a subset \(R'\) of \(R\). Taking up again the notation of loc. cit., one sees by Exp. XXII, 5.6.7 (ii) that \(U_i \cap H = \prod_{\alpha \in R_i \cap R'} U_\alpha\), hence that \((U_i \cap H)/(U_{i+1} \cap H)\) is identified with \(\prod_{\alpha \in R',\, a(\alpha) = i+1} U_\alpha\), which entails the result.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.10

In the situation of 2.9, the statements 2.2, 2.5, 2.6, 2.7 are equally valid for the group \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P) \cap H\).

pages.title: 3. Scheme of the parabolic subgroups of a reductive group

blocks.html: 3. Scheme of the parabolic subgroups of a reductive group

Let \(E\) be a finite twisted constant \(S\)-prescheme (Exp. X, 5.1). Consider the \(S\)-functor \(\mathscr{B}(E)\), where \(\mathscr{B}(E)(S')\) is the set of open and closed subpreschemes of \(E_{S'}\) (or, what amounts to the same, the set of open and closed subsets of \(E_{S'}\)); then \(\mathscr{B}(E)\) is representable by a finite twisted constant \(S\)-prescheme. Indeed, if \(E = \mathrm{A}_S\), where \(\mathrm{A}\) is a finite set, one has at once \(\mathscr{B}(E) \simeq \mathscr{P}(\mathrm{A})_S\), and one concludes by descent of open and closed subpreschemes. One evidently has: \[ \mathscr{B}(E_{S'}) = \mathscr{B}(E)_{S'}, \qquad \mathscr{B}(E \times_S E') = \mathscr{B}(E) \times_S \mathscr{B}(E'). \]

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group. The functor \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G)\) of the parabolic subgroups of \(G\) is defined by \[ \underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G)(S') = \text{set of parabolic subgroups of } G_{S'}. \] In particular \(G \in \underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G)(S)\), \(\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(G) \subset \underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G)\). We propose to define a morphism \[ \mathbf{t} : \underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G) \longrightarrow \mathscr{B}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)) \] possessing the following properties:
(i) \(\mathbf{t}\) is functorial in \(G\) (with respect to isomorphisms) and commutes with base extension.

(ii) If \((T, M, R, R_0, \ldots)\) is a pinning of \(G\) adapted to the parabolic subgroup \(P\) (1.11), the canonical isomorphism \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G) \simeq (R_0)_S\) (Exp. XXIV, 3.4 (iii)) transforms \(\mathbf{t}(P)\) into \(R_0(P)_S\) (notation of 1.11, 1.12).

Let first \(P\) be a parabolic subgroup of \(G\) and \((T, M, R, R_0, \ldots)\) a pinning of \(G\) adapted to \(P\). One defines \(\mathbf{t}(P)\) by (ii); the subprescheme \(\mathbf{t}(P)\) of \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)\) so constructed is independent of the chosen pinning. Indeed, if \((T', M', R', R'_0, \ldots)\) is another pinning of \(G\) adapted to \(P\), the unique inner automorphism of \(G\) transforming the first pinning into the second comes from \(P\) (1.15); the canonical isomorphism \(R_0 \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } R'_0\) therefore transforms \(R_0(P)\) into \(R'_0(P)\), which entails the announced result.

If now one no longer necessarily assumes \((G, P)\) pinnable, it follows at once from 1.14 and from the definition of \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)\) (Exp. XXIV, 3.3) that one can define by descent an open and closed subprescheme \(\mathbf{t}(P)\) of \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)\), unique, such that for every \(S' \to S\) for which \((G, P)_{S'}\) is pinnable, one has \(\mathbf{t}(P)_{S'} = \mathbf{t}(P_{S'})\).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 3.3

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \[ \mathbf{t} : \underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G) \longrightarrow \mathscr{B}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)) \] the morphism defined above.

(i) In order that two parabolic subgroups \(P\) and \(P'\) of \(G\) be conjugate locally for the (fpqc) topology (cf. 1.3), it is necessary and sufficient that \(\mathbf{t}(P) = \mathbf{t}(P')\).

(ii) \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G)\) is representable, and the morphism \(\mathbf{t}\) is smooth, projective, with integral geometric fibres.

By virtue of 3.2 (i), and of the fact that the inner automorphisms of \(G\) act trivially on \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)\) (Exp. XXIV, 3.4 (iv)), one indeed has \(\mathbf{t}(P) = \mathbf{t}(P')\) when \(P\) and \(P'\) are conjugate. Conversely, let \(P\) and \(P'\) be two parabolic subgroups of \(G\) such that \(\mathbf{t}(P) = \mathbf{t}(P')\); let us prove that \(P\) and \(P'\) are conjugate in \(G\), locally for the (fpqc) topology; one may first assume the couples \((G, P)\) and \((G, P')\) pinnable (1.14); by conjugacy of the pinnings in \(G\) (Exp. XXIV, 1.5), one may assume that there exists a pinning \((T, M, R, R_0)\) of \(G\) adapted to \(P\) and \(P'\). Then \(\mathbf{t}(P) = \mathbf{t}(P')\) implies \(R_0(P) = R_0(P')\), hence \(P = P'\) (cf. 1.4 (v)). We have thus proved (i). To prove (ii), let us take up again the notation of Exp. XXII, 5.11.5.

One has a canonical morphism \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G) \to \mathscr{H}_c\), and it is clear (for example by reduction to the pinned case) that it fits into a cartesian square (where the vertical arrows are monomorphisms) \[ \xymatrix{ \underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G) \ar[r]^-{\mathbf{t}} \ar@{^{(}->}[d] & \mathscr{B}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)) \ar@{^{(}->}[d] \\ \mathscr{H}_c \ar[r]^-{c\ell} & \mathscr{C}\ell_c. } \] Now (loc. cit.) \(\mathscr{H}_c\) is representable and the morphism \(c\ell\) is smooth, quasi-projective, of finite presentation, with integral geometric fibres, hence so also is \(\mathbf{t}\).

It remains to prove that \(\mathbf{t}\) is proper; but this is now a local assertion for the (fpqc) topology, and one may reduce to the pinned case \(G = (G, T, M, R, R_0, \ldots)\). One then has \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G) \simeq (R_0)_S\), and it suffices to prove that for every subset \(R_1\) of \(R_0\), the \(S\)-prescheme \(\mathbf{t}^{-1}((R_1)_S)\) is proper over \(S\). Now if \(P_1\) is the parabolic subgroup of \(G\) containing \(T\) such that \(R_0(P_1) = R_1\), it follows from (i) that the morphism \(G \to \underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G)\) defined set-theoretically by \(g \mapsto \mathrm{int}(g)P_1\) induces an isomorphism of \(G/\underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(P_1)\) onto \(\mathbf{t}^{-1}((R_1)_S)\). Now (1.2), \(G/\underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(P_1) = G/P_1\) is projective over \(S\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.4

\(\mathscr{B}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G))\) is called the scheme of types of parabolics of \(G\); \(\mathbf{t}(P)\) is called the type of \(P\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.5

The \(S\)-functor \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G)\) is representable by an \(S\)-prescheme smooth and projective over \(S\). The decomposition \[ \underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G) \longrightarrow \mathscr{B}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)) \longrightarrow S \] is the Stein factorisation (EGA III, 4.3.3) of the structural morphism \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G) \to S\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.6

For each \(t \in \mathscr{B}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G))(S)\), the \(S\)-prescheme \[ \underline{\mathrm{Par}}_t(G) = \mathbf{t}^{-1}(t) \] of the parabolic subgroups of \(G\) of type \(t\) is smooth and projective over \(S\), homogeneous under \(G\). If \(P\) is a parabolic subgroup of \(G\), one has a canonical isomorphism \(G/P \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \underline{\mathrm{Par}}_{\mathbf{t}(P)}(G)\). One has \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}_\emptyset(G) = \underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(G)\), \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}_{\mathrm{Dyn}(G)}(G) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } S\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.7

The \(S\)-scheme \(\mathscr{B}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G))\) is endowed with a natural order structure (the domination relation, here set-theoretic inclusion, between subpreschemes).

This order structure is a lattice; in particular the infimum of two open and closed subpreschemes of \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)_{S'}\) is evidently their intersection. Let us moreover remark that if \(B\) is a Borel subgroup of \(G\), one can define the functor \(X\) of the parabolic subgroups of \(G\) containing \(B\). The morphism \(X \to \mathscr{B}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G))\) induced by \(\mathbf{t}\) is an isomorphism (for the structure of "ordered scheme"), by virtue of the assertion \(P \subset Q \Rightarrow \mathbf{t}(P) \subset \mathbf{t}(Q)\) and of:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.8

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\), \(t'\) a section of \(\mathscr{B}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G))\) over \(S\), such that \(\mathbf{t}(P) \subset t'\). There exists a unique parabolic subgroup \(P'\) of \(G\), containing \(P\), and such that \(\mathbf{t}(P') = t'\).

After possibly extending the base, one may assume that \(P\) contains a Borel subgroup \(B\) of \(G\). The uniqueness of \(P'\) then follows from 1.17. To prove the existence, one may place oneself in the split case, in which case the assertion is evident, cf. no 1.

blocks.title: Remarks
blocks.html:
Remarks 3.8.1

(i) The assertion analogous to 3.8 obtained by reversing the inclusions is evidently false. It would entail for example that every group of type \(\mathrm{A}_1\) possesses a Borel group, which is not the case, cf. Exp. XX, no 5.

(ii) It follows at once from what precedes that \(\mathbf{t}(P) \subset \mathbf{t}(Q)\) means that locally for (fpqc) or (ét), \(P\) is conjugate to a subgroup of \(Q\) (it suffices moreover to verify the assertion on the geometric fibres). Furthermore, we shall see in no 5 that one can replace the étale topology by the Zariski topology.

The preceding discussions can be taken up again in the case of critical subgroups. Let us recall (Exp. XXII, 5.10.4 and 5.10.5) that a reductive subgroup \(H\) of the reductive group \(G\) is critical if \(H = \underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(\mathrm{rad}(H))\), that a subtorus \(Q\) of \(G\) is a critical torus if \(Q = \mathrm{rad}(\underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q))\) and that critical subgroups and critical tori are in one-to-one correspondence (by \(H \mapsto \mathrm{rad}(H)\) and \(Q \mapsto \underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q)\)).

If \((G, T, M, R)\) is a split \(S\)-group, the subgroup of \(G\) containing \(T\) corresponding to the subset \(R'\) of \(R\) (Exp. XXII, 5.4.2) is critical if and only if \(R'\) is "vectorial" (that is to say the intersection of \(R\) with a vector subspace of \(M \otimes \mathbf{Q}\)), cf. Exp. XXII, 5.10.6.

If \(G\) is an arbitrary reductive \(S\)-group, one defines, as in Exp. XXII, 5.11.5, a finite étale \(S\)-prescheme \(\mathscr{C}\ell_{\mathrm{crit}}\), which in the split case will be the constant scheme associated with the set of vectorial subsets of \(R\) modulo the action of the Weyl group. If \(\underline{\mathrm{Crit}}(G)\) denotes the "functor of the critical subgroups" of \(G\), one will have a canonical morphism \(\underline{\mathrm{Crit}}(G) \xrightarrow{\ c\ell\ } \mathscr{C}\ell_{\mathrm{crit}}\), which will fit into a cartesian diagram \[ \xymatrix{ \underline{\mathrm{Crit}}(G) \ar[r]^-{c\ell} \ar@{^{(}->}[d] & \mathscr{C}\ell_{\mathrm{crit}} \ar@{^{(}->}[d] \\ \mathscr{H}_c \ar[r]^-{c\ell} & \mathscr{C}\ell_c. } \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.10

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(\underline{\mathrm{Crit}}(G)\) the functor of its critical subgroups, \(\mathscr{C}\ell_{\mathrm{crit}}\) the finite étale \(S\)-scheme defined above, \[ c\ell : \underline{\mathrm{Crit}}(G) \longrightarrow \mathscr{C}\ell_{\mathrm{crit}} \] the morphism defined above.

(i) In order that the critical subgroups \(H\) and \(H'\) of \(G\) be conjugate (locally for the (fpqc) topology, it is necessary and sufficient that \(c\ell(H) = c\ell(H')\).

(ii) \(\underline{\mathrm{Crit}}(G)\) is representable and the morphism \(c\ell\) is smooth, affine, with integral geometric fibres.

This is proved as 3.3 except for the assertion "\(c\ell\) is affine". It suffices to prove that \(\underline{\mathrm{Crit}}(G)\) is affine over \(S\). Now \(\underline{\mathrm{Crit}}(G)\) is naturally identified with the \(S\)-functor of the critical tori of \(G\), and one therefore has a canonical monomorphism \[ \underline{\mathrm{Crit}}(G) \longrightarrow \mathrm{M} \] where \(\mathrm{M}\) is the prescheme of the subgroups of multiplicative type of \(G\) (Exp. XI, 4.1). To prove that \(\underline{\mathrm{Crit}}(G)\) is affine over \(S\), it suffices, by virtue of Exp. XII 5.3, to show that this morphism is an open and closed immersion, or again, on making the base change \(\mathrm{M} \to S\), to prove the following assertion: if \(Q\) is a subgroup of multiplicative type of the reductive group \(G\), the \(S' \to S\) such that \(Q_{S'}\) is a critical torus of \(G_{S'}\) are those which factor through a certain open and closed subprescheme of \(S\). Now to say that \(Q\) is a critical torus is to say:
(1) that \(Q\) is a torus,
(2) \(Q\) being a torus, that \(\mathrm{rad}(\underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q))\), which is also a torus, is of the same relative dimension as \(Q\).
Now these two conditions are indeed of the type envisaged.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.11

The \(S\)-functor \(\underline{\mathrm{Crit}}(G)\) is representable by an \(S\)-prescheme smooth and affine over \(S\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.12

Let \(H\) be a critical subgroup of the reductive \(S\)-group \(G\). Then \(G/\underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(H)\) and \(G/H\) are representable by \(S\)-preschemes affine and smooth over \(S\).
The first assertion follows from 3.11, the second from the first and from Exp. XXII, 5.10.2.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.13

Let \(Q\) be a subtorus of the reductive \(S\)-group \(G\). Then \(G/\underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q)\) is representable by an \(S\)-prescheme smooth and affine over \(S\). The same holds for \(G/\underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(Q)\) if \(Q\) is a critical subtorus of \(G\).

Indeed, \(H = \underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q)\) is critical (Exp. XXII, 5.10.5), and one has \(\underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(H) = \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(Q)\) if \(Q\) is critical (loc. cit. 5.10.8).

By virtue of the conjugacy of the Levi subgroups of the parabolic subgroups of \(G\), there exists a unique morphism \[ u : \mathscr{B}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)) \longrightarrow \mathscr{C}\ell_{\mathrm{crit}} \] such that for every parabolic subgroup \(P\) of \(G\), and every Levi subgroup \(L\) of \(P\), one has \(c\ell(L) = u(\mathbf{t}(P))\), and such that this remains true after any base change.

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group. Consider the following \(S\)-functors: \[ \begin{aligned} \underline{\mathrm{PL}}(S') &= \{\text{pairs } P \supset L,\ P \text{ parabolic in } G_{S'},\ L \text{ Levi subgroup of } P\}; \\ \underline{\mathrm{PT}}(S') &= \{\text{pairs } P \supset T,\ P \text{ parabolic in } G_{S'},\ T \text{ maximal torus of } P\}; \\ \underline{\mathrm{LT}}(S') &= \{\text{pairs } L \supset T,\ L \text{ critical subgroup of } G_{S'},\ T \text{ maximal torus of } L\}; \\ \underline{\mathrm{PLT}}(S') &= \{\text{triples } P \supset L \subset T,\ P \text{ parabolic in } G_{S'},\ L \text{ Levi subgroup of } P, \\ &\hphantom{{}= \{\text{triples } P \supset L \subset T,\ } T \text{ maximal torus of } L\}. \end{aligned} \] One has evident morphisms between these functors and the functors \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G)\), \(\underline{\mathrm{Crit}}(G)\), \(\underline{\mathrm{Tor}}(G)\) already introduced, and one has a commutative diagram in the shape of a truncated cube (see figure). \[ \xymatrix@C=1.2em@R=1.6em{ & \underline{\mathrm{LT}} \ar[dl]_{a\ \text{(aff.)}} \ar[dd]^(0.3){k\ \text{(ét.)}} & & \underline{\mathrm{PLT}} \ar[ll]_{g\ \text{(ét.)}} \ar[dl]^{b\ \text{(aff.)}} \ar[dd]^{\wr\ e\ \text{(isom.)}} \\ \underline{\mathrm{Crit}}(G) \ar[ddd]_{c\ell\ \text{(aff.)}} & & \underline{\mathrm{PL}} \ar[ll]_(0.4){f\ \text{(ét.)}} \ar[ddddd]^(0.65){d\ \text{(aff.)}} & \\ & \underline{\mathrm{Tor}}(G) \ar[ddd]^(0.4){r\ \text{(aff.)}} & & \underline{\mathrm{PT}} \ar[ll]_(0.35){h\ \text{(ét.)}} \ar[ddddl]^{c\ \text{(aff.)}} \\ & & & \\ \mathscr{C}\ell_{\mathrm{crit}} \ar[dr]^{q\ \text{(ét.)}} & & & \\ & S & & \\ \mathscr{B}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)) \ar[uu]^{u\ \text{(ét.)}} \ar[ur]_{p\ \text{(ét.)}} & & \underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G) \ar[ll]^{\mathbf{t}\ \text{(proj.)}} & } \]
Figure 3.15.1

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 3.16

(cf. figure 3.15.1).

(i) All the morphisms of the diagram are smooth, surjective, and of finite presentation.

(ii) All the morphisms of the diagram, with the exception of \(\mathbf{t}\), are affine; the morphism \(\mathbf{t}\) is projective.

(iii) All the morphisms of the diagram are either finite étale, or with integral geometric fibres: the morphisms \(f\), \(g\), \(h\), \(k\), \(p\), \(q\) and \(u\) are finite étale, the morphisms \(a\), \(b\), \(c\), \(d\), \(r\) and \(c\ell\) have integral geometric fibres, the morphism \(e\) is an isomorphism.

(iv) The square \((a, b, f, g)\) is cartesian.
Proof. It is first of all clear that \(e\) is an isomorphism, by 1.6 (ii). On the other hand, (iv) is evident.

The morphism \(a\) is smooth, affine, with integral geometric fibres: indeed, by the base change \(\underline{\mathrm{Crit}}(G) \to S\), it suffices to verify that the morphism \(\underline{\mathrm{Tor}}(\mathrm{L}_0) \to S\), where \(\mathrm{L}_0\) is the universal critical subgroup, possesses these properties; now \(\mathrm{L}_0\) is reductive (by definition), and one is reduced to Exp. XXII, 5.8.3. The morphism \(b\) therefore possesses the same properties, by virtue of (iv).

The morphism \(d\) is likewise smooth, affine, with integral geometric fibres, by virtue of 1.9; the same therefore holds for \(c = dbe^{-1}\). The morphism \(r\) possesses these same properties (Exp. XXII, 5.8.3), as does the morphism \(c\ell\) (3.10).

On the other hand, we have already proved that the morphisms \(p\) and \(q\) are finite étale surjective (3.1 and 3.9). If we prove that \(f\) and \(k\) are finite étale surjective, the same properties will hold for \(g\) (by (iv)) and for \(h\) (by \(h = kge^{-1}\)); since the stated properties of \(\mathbf{t}\) were proved in 3.3 (ii), it therefore only remains for us to prove that \(f\) (resp. \(k\)) is finite étale surjective; let us give the proof for \(k\), that for \(f\) being analogous.

It suffices for us to prove that if \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(G\), the functor \(\underline{\mathrm{C}}\) of the critical subgroups of \(G\) containing \(T\) is representable by a finite étale \(S\)-scheme with non-empty fibres; one may assume \(G\) split with respect to \(T\); let then \(E\) be the set of vectorial subsets of \(R\) (root system of the splitting); \(\underline{\mathrm{C}}\) is representable by \(E_S\) (3.9), which completes the proof.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.17

All the functors of the preceding diagram are representable by \(S\)-preschemes smooth over \(S\), and they are all affine over \(S\), with the exception of \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G)\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.18

(i) The fact that the morphism \(f : \underline{\mathrm{PL}} \to \underline{\mathrm{Crit}}(G)\) is étale surjective entails that a subgroup of \(G\) is critical if and only if it is, locally for the étale topology, a Levi subgroup of a parabolic subgroup of \(G\).

On the other hand, one must not believe that in general the map \(f(S) : \underline{\mathrm{PL}}(S) \to \underline{\mathrm{Crit}}(G)(S)\) is surjective: it may very well happen that a critical subgroup \(L\) of \(G\) does not come over \(S\) from a parabolic subgroup of \(G\); for example, a maximal torus is not always contained in a Borel group (example: a non-split form of \(\mathrm{SL}_2\), cf. Exp. XX, no 5).

(ii) Likewise, it may happen that the morphism \(u : \mathscr{B}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)) \to \mathscr{C}\ell_{\mathrm{crit}}\) is not an isomorphism: two parabolic subgroups of distinct types may have Levi subgroups of the same type; example: in a group of type \(\mathrm{A}_2\), there are two types of parabolic subgroups whose Levi subgroups are of semi-simple rank 1 (corresponding to the two vertices of the diagram), whereas there is only a single type of critical subgroups of rank 1.

The analogous example with a group of type \(\mathrm{A}_3\) shows that, even over an algebraically closed field, non-isomorphic parabolic subgroups may have Levi subgroups of the same type.
Let us end this no with an application to the theory of principal bundles.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3.20

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(F\) a principal homogeneous bundle under \(G\), \(G^F\) the corresponding twisted form of \(G\). Let us identify \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)\) and \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G^F)\) (Exp. XXIV, 3.5). Let \(P\) be a parabolic subgroup of \(G\). One has a canonical isomorphism \[ F/P \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \underline{\mathrm{Par}}_{\mathbf{t}(P)}(G^F). \] In particular, in order that the structural group of \(F\) can be reduced to \(P\), it is necessary and sufficient that \(G^F\) possess a parabolic subgroup of type \(\mathbf{t}(P)\).
The proof is carried out exactly as in Exp. XXIV, 4.2.1.

If \(S\) is a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, and if \(t \in \mathscr{B}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G))(S)\), one denotes by \(\mathrm{H}^1_t(S, G)\) the subset of \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, G)\) formed of the classes of principal bundles \(F\) under \(G\) such that the associated group \(G^F\) possesses a parabolic subgroup of type \(t\). If \(G\) itself possesses a parabolic subgroup \(P\) of type \(t\), \(\mathrm{H}^1_t(S, G)\) is none other than the image of \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, P)\) in \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, G)\), an image which therefore does not depend on the chosen \(P\).

pages.title: 4. Relative position of two parabolic groups

blocks.html: 4. Relative position of two parabolic groups
4.1. A preliminary result

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.1.1

Let \(k\) be a field, \(G\) a reductive \(k\)-group, \(P\) and \(P'\) two parabolic subgroups of \(G\). Then \(P \cap P'\) is smooth, of the same reductive rank as \(G\) and contains a maximal torus \(T\) of \(G\).

Let us first assume \(k\) algebraically closed. Let \(B\) (resp. \(B'\)) be a Borel subgroup of \(P\) (resp. \(P'\)). It is known that there exists \(g \in G(k)\) with \(\mathrm{int}(g)B = B'\). On the other hand, if \(T_0\) is a maximal torus of \(B\) and if one puts \(\mathrm{N} = \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(T_0)\), it is known (Bruhat's theorem, BIBLE, 13-11, cor. 1 to th. 3) that \(G(k) = B(k)\mathrm{N}(k)B(k)\). One thus sees that there exist \(b, b_1 \in B(k)\) and \(n \in \mathrm{N}(k)\) such that \(g = bnb_1\), hence \(\mathrm{int}(b)\,\mathrm{int}(n)B = B'\). One then has \[ P \cap P' \supset B \cap B' = \mathrm{int}(b)(B \cap \mathrm{int}(n)B') \supset \mathrm{int}(b)T_0. \]

Let us now assume \(k\) arbitrary. Applying the preceding result, one sees that \(P_{\overline{k}} \cap P'_{\overline{k}}\) contains a maximal torus of \(G_{\overline{k}}\); by Exp. XXII, 5.4.5, one deduces that \((P \cap P')_{\overline{k}}\) is smooth "along the unit section", hence smooth since one is over a field (Exp. VIB), hence that \(P \cap P'\) is smooth. By Exp. VIA 2.3.1, the identity component \((P \cap P')^0\) of \(P \cap P'\) is therefore an open subgroup of \(P \cap P'\), smooth over \(S\). One may then apply Exp. XIV, 1.1 to it.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 4.1.2

One can prove ([BT], 4.5) that \(P \cap P'\) is connected. We shall not use this fact.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 4.1.3

The preceding lemma is not true over an arbitrary prescheme. Indeed, let for example \(G\) be a reductive group over an algebraically closed field \(k\), and let \(B\) be a Borel group of \(G\). Let us take \(G = X\) as base and consider the Borel subgroups \(B_1\) and \(B_2\) of \(G_X\), where \(B_1 = B_X\) and \(B_2 = \mathrm{int}(g_0)B_1\), \(g_0\) being the canonical (diagonal) section of \(G_X\). For each \(g \in X(k)\), the fibre of \(B_1 \cap B_2\) at \(g\) is none other than \(B \cap \mathrm{int}(g)B\). If one assumes \(B \neq G\), the dimension of this fibre varies with \(g\), hence \(B_1 \cap B_2\) cannot be smooth over \(X\).
4.2. Transversal position

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 4.2.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) and \(Q\) two parabolic subgroups of \(G\). The following conditions on the couple \((P, Q)\) are equivalent:

(i) \(\mathrm{Lie}(P/S) + \mathrm{Lie}(Q/S) = \mathrm{Lie}(G/S)\).

(ii) The canonical morphism \(P \times_S Q \to G\) is smooth.

(ii′) The canonical morphism \(P \to G/Q\) is smooth.

(iii) The canonical morphism \(P \times_S Q \to G\) is open.

(iii′) The canonical morphism \(P \to G/Q\) is open.

(iv) The canonical morphism \(P \times_S Q \to G\) is dominant fibre by fibre.

(iv′) The canonical morphism \(P \to G/Q\) is dominant fibre by fibre.

(v) For every \(s \in S\), "\(P_{\overline{s}} \cap Q_{\overline{s}}\) is of minimum dimension", i.e. one has \[ \dim(P_{\overline{s}} \cap Q_{\overline{s}}) = \dim P_{\overline{s}} + \dim Q_{\overline{s}} - \dim G_{\overline{s}}. \]

(vi) There exists a covering family for the étale topology \(\{S_i \to S\}\), and for each \(i\) a Borel group \(B_i\) of \(P_{S_i}\) and a Borel group \(B'_i\) of \(Q_{S_i}\), such that \(B_i \cap B'_i\) is a maximal torus of \(G_{S_i}\).

(vii) There exists a covering family for the étale topology \(\{S_i \to S\}\), and for each \(i\) a splitting \((T_i, \ldots, R_i)\) of \(G_{S_i}\) and a system of positive roots \(R_{+i}\) of \(R_i\), such that \(P_{S_i}\) (resp. \(Q_{S_i}\)) is the subgroup of type (R) of \(G_{S_i}\) containing \(T_i\) and defined by a subset \(R_i^{(1)}\) (resp. \(R_i^{(2)}\)) of \(R\) containing \(R_{+i}\) (resp. \(-R_{+i}\)) (see Exp. XXII, 5.4.2 and 5.2.1 for the definitions).

Proof. We shall prove the theorem following the logical diagram \[ \xymatrix@C=1.6em@R=1.6em{ \text{(i)} \ar@{=>}[d] & \text{(vii)} \ar@{=>}[l] & \text{(vi)} & \\ \text{(ii}'\text{)} \ar@{=>}[d] \ar@{=>}[r] & \text{(iii}'\text{)} \ar@{=>}[r] & \text{(iv}'\text{)} \ar@{=>}[r] & \text{(v)} \ar@{=>}[ul] \\ \text{(ii)} \ar@{=>}[r] & \text{(iii)} \ar@{=>}[r] & \text{(iv)} \ar@{=>}[ur] & } \]

One has trivially (ii) \(\Rightarrow\) (iii) and (ii′) \(\Rightarrow\) (iii′). If (iii) is satisfied, the set-theoretic image of the morphism \(P \times_S Q \Rightarrow G\) is an open subset of \(G\) which contains the unit section; since the fibres of \(G\) are connected, this image is dense on each fibre, which proves (iv). One has likewise (iii′) \(\Rightarrow\) (iv′).
One has (ii′) \(\Rightarrow\) (ii), by virtue of the cartesian diagram \[ \xymatrix{ P \times_S Q \ar[r] \ar[d]_{\mathrm{pr}_1} & G \ar[d] \\ P \ar[r] & G/Q. } \]

On the other hand (iv) or (iv′) entails (v), by virtue of dimension theory (cf. EGA IV\(_2\), 5.6.6). One will note that one may indeed assume \(S = \mathrm{Spec}(k)\), \(k\) an algebraically closed field, and that every non-empty fibre of the morphism (iv), resp. (iv′), at a point of \(G(k)\), resp. of \((G/Q)(k)\), is isomorphic to \(P \cap Q\) (as an immediate computation shows).
One has (vi) \(\Rightarrow\) (vii), by Exp. XXII, 5.5.1 (iv) and 5.9.2.

One has (vii) \(\Rightarrow\) (i), for in order to verify that \(\mathrm{Lie}(P) + \mathrm{Lie}(Q) = \mathrm{Lie}(G)\), one may argue locally for (fpqc), hence, if (vii) is satisfied, assume \(G\) split, \(P \supset B_{R_+}\) and \(Q \supset B_{-R_+}\) (usual notation), in which case one already has \[ \mathrm{Lie}(B_{R_+}) + \mathrm{Lie}(B_{-R_+}) = \mathrm{Lie}(G). \] Let us prove that (i) implies (ii′).

Let \(u : P \to G/Q\) be the canonical morphism; to prove that \(u\) is smooth, one may content oneself with doing so for the geometric fibres of \(u\), since \(P\) and \(G/Q\) are smooth over \(S\), and one may therefore assume that \(S\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field. Since the morphism \(u\) is compatible with the evident action of \(P\) (one has \(u(pp') = pu(p')\)) and since \(P\) is connected, it suffices (Exp. VIB) to verify that \(u\) is smooth at \(e \in G(k)\), to verify that \(u\) is smooth at \(e \in P(k)\), i.e. (SGA 1, II 4.7) that the tangent map to \(u\) at \(e\) is surjective; but the latter is naturally identified with the canonical map \(\mathrm{Lie}(P) \to \mathrm{Lie}(G)/\mathrm{Lie}(Q)\), which is surjective if (i) is satisfied.

It therefore only remains for us to verify the last assertion, that is to say (v) \(\Rightarrow\) (vi). Let us first assume that \(S\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field. By 4.1.1, there exists a maximal torus \(T\) contained in \(P\) and \(Q\); let \(R\) (resp. \(R_1\), resp. \(R_2\)) be the set of roots of \(G\) (resp. \(P\), resp. \(Q\)) relative to \(T\).

One has: \[ \begin{aligned} &\dim(G) = \dim(T) + \mathrm{Card}(R), \qquad &&\dim(P) = \dim(T) + \mathrm{Card}(R_1), \\ &\dim(Q) = \dim(T) + \mathrm{Card}(R_2), \qquad &&\dim(P \cap Q) = \dim(T) + \mathrm{Card}(R_1 \cap R_2), \end{aligned} \] by Exp. XXII, 5.4.4 and 5.4.5 for example. The condition of (v) is therefore equivalent to \[ \mathrm{Card}(R_1 \cap R_2) = \mathrm{Card}(R_1) + \mathrm{Card}(R_2) - \mathrm{Card}(R). \] that is to say \(R_1 \cup R_2 = R\). To prove (vi), it suffices, by virtue of Exp. XXII, 5.9.2 and 5.4.5, to prove that \(R_1 \cap -R_2\) contains a system of positive roots of \(R\). One is therefore reduced to proving:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.2.2

Let \(R\) be a "root system" (for example the set of roots of a root datum in the sense of Exposé XXI). Let \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) be two closed subsets of \(R\) each containing a system of positive roots. If \(R_1 \cup R_2 = R\), then \(R_1 \cap -R_2\) contains a system of positive roots.

Indeed, since \(R_1 \cap -R_2 = R_3\) is evidently closed, and by virtue of Exp. XXI, 3.3.6, it suffices to show that \(R_3 \cup -R_3 = R\). Now it is known that \(R_1 \cup -R_1 = R = R_2 \cup -R_2\), and one concludes thanks to the following elementary fact: if \(\mathrm{A}\), \(\mathrm{A}'\), \(B\), \(B'\) are four subsets of a set \(E\), and if \(\mathrm{A} \cup \mathrm{A}' = B \cup B' = \mathrm{A} \cup B = \mathrm{A}' \cup B' = E\), one has \((\mathrm{A} \cap B') \cup (\mathrm{A}' \cap B) = E\).

This completes the proof of (v) \(\Rightarrow\) (vi) in the case where the base is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field. Let us now return to the general case and assume (v) satisfied. Let \(s \in S\); by virtue of what precedes, one can find a Borel subgroup \(\overline{B}\) (resp. \(\overline{B}'\)) of \(P_{\overline{s}}\) (resp. \(Q_{\overline{s}}\)) such that \(\overline{B} \cap \overline{B}'\) is a maximal torus of \(G_{\overline{s}}\).

Since the \(S\)-prescheme \(\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(P) \simeq \underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(P/\mathrm{rad}^u(P))\) of the Borel subgroups of \(P\) is smooth, one may, applying Exp. XI, 1.10 and arguing locally for the étale topology (i.e. replacing \(S\) by an \(S' \to S\) étale and covering \(s\), and \(s\) by a point of its fibre in \(S'\)), assume that there exists a Borel subgroup \(B\) of \(P\) projecting onto \(\overline{B}\); one may likewise assume that there exists a Borel subgroup \(B'\) of \(Q\) projecting onto \(\overline{B}'\). Since \(\overline{B} \cap \overline{B}'\) is a maximal torus of \(G\), there exists an open subset \(U\) of \(S\) containing \(s\) and such that \(B_U \cap B'_U\) is a maximal torus of \(G_U\) (Exp. XXII, 5.9.4), which proves (vi). Q.E.D.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 4.2.3

A couple \((P, Q)\) satisfying the equivalent conditions (i) to (vii) of theorem 4.2.1 is said to be in transversal position. One also says that \(P\) is in transversal position relative to \(Q\), or, by abuse of language, that \(P\) and \(Q\) are in (mutual) transversal position.
In view of (vi), this definition coincides in the case of Borel groups with that of Exp. XXII, 5.9.1.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.2.4

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) and \(Q\) two parabolic subgroups of \(G\).

(i) In order that \((P, Q)\) be in transversal position, it is necessary and sufficient that for each point \(s\) of \(S\), the couple \((P_{\overline{s}}, Q_{\overline{s}})\) be in transversal position; if \(S' \to S\) is a surjective morphism, and if \((P_{S'}, Q_{S'})\) is in transversal position, then \((P, Q)\) is in transversal position.

(ii) There exists an open subprescheme \(U\) of \(S\) satisfying the following property: in order that a morphism \(S' \to S\) factor through \(U\), it is necessary and sufficient that \((P_{S'}, Q_{S'})\) be in transversal position.

(iii) Consider the subfunctors \[ \begin{aligned} \underline{\mathrm{Gen}}(G) &\subset \underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G) \times_S \underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G) \\ \underline{\mathrm{Gen}}(/Q) &\subset \underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G) \\ \underline{\mathrm{Gen}}(P/Q) &\subset G \end{aligned} \] defined as follows: for \(S' \to S\), \(\underline{\mathrm{Gen}}(G)(S')\) is the set of couples of parabolic subgroups of \(G_{S'}\) in transversal position, \(\underline{\mathrm{Gen}}(/Q)(S')\) is the set of parabolic subgroups of \(G_{S'}\) in transversal position relative to \(Q_{S'}\), \(\underline{\mathrm{Gen}}(P/Q)(S')\) is the set of \(g \in G(S')\) such that \(\mathrm{int}(g)P_{S'}\) is in transversal position relative to \(Q_{S'}\).

Each of these functors is representable by a relatively dense open subprescheme (cf. Exp. XVIII § 1) of the corresponding \(S\)-prescheme \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G) \times_S \underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G)\), resp. \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G)\), resp. \(G\).

Assertions (i) follow at once from the description 4.2.1 (i) of the term "transversal position". To prove (ii), one takes \(U = S - \mathrm{Supp}(\mathrm{Coker}\, u)\) where \(u\) is the canonical morphism \(\mathrm{Lie}(P) \oplus \mathrm{Lie}(G) \to \mathrm{Lie}(G)\).

Since we have cartesian diagrams \[ \xymatrix{ G \ar[r]^-{f} & \underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G) \\ \underline{\mathrm{Gen}}(P/Q) \ar[r] \ar@{^{(}->}[u] & \underline{\mathrm{Gen}}(/Q) \ar@{^{(}->}[u] } \qquad \xymatrix{ \underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G) \ar[r]^-{f'} & \underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G) \times_S \underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G) \\ \underline{\mathrm{Gen}}(/Q) \ar[r] \ar@{^{(}->}[u] & \underline{\mathrm{Gen}}(G) \ar@{^{(}->}[u] } \] (where \(f(g) = \mathrm{int}(g)P\) and \(f'(R) = (R, Q)\)), it suffices to verify (iii) in the case of \(\underline{\mathrm{Gen}}(G)\).

Let then \(P_0\) be the canonical parabolic subgroup of \(G_{\underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G)}\); set \[ X = \underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G) \times_S \underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G), \qquad P = \mathrm{pr}_1^*(P_0) \quad \text{and} \quad Q = \mathrm{pr}_2^*(P_0); \] applying assertion (ii) to the parabolic subgroups \(P\) and \(Q\) of \(G_X\), one constructs an open sub-prescheme \(U\) of \(X\), which, as one verifies at once, is indeed identified with \(\underline{\mathrm{Gen}}(G)\). It remains to verify the density assertion, which can be done on the geometric fibres; we may therefore assume \(S = \mathrm{Spec}(k)\), \(k\) an algebraically closed field; since \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G)\) is smooth, it suffices to verify that \(\underline{\mathrm{Gen}}(G)\) meets each irreducible component of \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G) \times_S \underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G)\); in other words, by 3.3, it suffices to see that if \(t\), \(t' \in \mathscr{B}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G))(S)\), there exists a pair \((P, P')\) in transversal position, with \(\mathbf{t}(P) = t\), \(\mathbf{t}(P') = t'\). Now this is immediate: one chooses a pair \((B, B')\) of Borel groups of \(G\) such that \(B \cap B'\) is a maximal torus (one splits \(G\) and applies Exp. XXII, 5.9.2), then applies 3.8 to construct \(P \supset B\) and \(P' \supset B'\), with \(\mathbf{t}(P) = t\), \(\mathbf{t}(P') = t'\); \(P\) and \(P'\) are of the desired types and are in transversal position by 4.2.1 (vi).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.2.5

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) and \(Q\) two parabolic subgroups of \(G\), the pair \((P, Q)\) being in transversal position.

(i) Let \(P'\) and \(Q'\) be two parabolic subgroups of \(G\), of the same type as \(P\) and \(Q\) respectively. In order that the pair \((P', Q')\) be in transversal position, it is necessary and sufficient that it be conjugate to the pair \((P, Q)\), locally for the étale topology. (N. B. We shall see in § 5 that the étale topology may be replaced by the Zariski topology).

(ii) The canonical morphism \(P \times_S Q \to G\) induces a smooth and surjective morphism \(P \times_S Q \to \underline{\mathrm{Gen}}(Q/P)\), and an isomorphism \(P \times_S Q/P \cap Q \simeq \underline{\mathrm{Gen}}(Q/P)\) (\(P \cap Q = R\) acting on \(P \times_S Q\) by \((p, q)r = (pr, r^{-1}q)\)).

(iii) The canonical morphism \(P \to \underline{\mathrm{Par}}_{\mathbf{t}(Q)}(G)\) (defined set-theoretically by \(p \mapsto \mathrm{int}(p)Q\)) induces a smooth and surjective morphism \(P \to \underline{\mathrm{Gen}}(/P) \bigcap \underline{\mathrm{Par}}_{\mathbf{t}(Q)}(G)\), and an isomorphism \[ P/(P \cap Q) \simeq \underline{\mathrm{Gen}}(/P) \bigcap \underline{\mathrm{Par}}_{\mathbf{t}(Q)}(G). \]

(iv) The canonical morphism \(G \to \underline{\mathrm{Par}}_{\mathbf{t}(P)}(G) \times_S \underline{\mathrm{Par}}_{\mathbf{t}(Q)}(G)\) (defined set-theoretically by \(g \mapsto (\mathrm{int}(g)P, \mathrm{int}(g)Q)\)) induces a smooth and surjective morphism \(G \to \underline{\mathrm{Gen}}(G) \bigcap (\underline{\mathrm{Par}}_{\mathbf{t}(P)}(G) \times_S \underline{\mathrm{Par}}_{\mathbf{t}(Q)}(G))\) and an isomorphism \[ G/(P \cap Q) \simeq \underline{\mathrm{Gen}}(G) \bigcap (\underline{\mathrm{Par}}_{\mathbf{t}(P)}(G) \times_S \underline{\mathrm{Par}}_{\mathbf{t}(Q)}(G)). \]

Let us prove (i). It is clear that the condition is sufficient; let us prove that it is necessary. So let \((P', Q')\) be in transversal position. Since \(P\) and \(P'\) are conjugate locally for the étale topology, we may assume \(P = P'\), and it suffices for us to prove that if \(Q\) and \(Q'\) are two parabolic subgroups of \(G\), in transversal position relative to \(P\), and of the same type, then they are conjugate, locally for the étale topology, by a section of \(P\). Using 4.2.1 (vi), we may assume that there exist Borel groups \(B\), \(B'\), \(B_1\), \(B'_1\) of \(P\), \(P\), \(Q\), \(Q'\) respectively, such that \(B \cap B_1 = T\) and \(B' \cap B'_1 = T'\) are maximal tori of \(G\). Now the Killing couples \((B, T)\) and \((B', T')\) of \(P\) are conjugate locally in \(P\) for the étale topology (1.16), and we may assume \(B = B'\), \(T = T'\), in which case \(B_1 = B'_1\) by Exp. XXII, 5.9.2, hence \(Q = Q'\) by 3.8.

Assertions (ii), (iii) and (iv) are proved in parallel fashion. Let us prove for example (ii); let \(g \in \underline{\mathrm{Gen}}(Q/P)(S)\), i.e. let \(g \in G(S)\) be such that \(\mathrm{int}(g)Q\) is in transversal position relative to \(P\). By virtue of the preceding proof, \(Q\) and \(\mathrm{int}(g)Q\) are conjugate locally for the étale topology, by a section of \(P\). Reasoning locally for this topology, we may assume that there exists \(p \in P(S)\) such that \(\mathrm{int}(g)Q = \mathrm{int}(p)Q\), hence \(p^{-1}g \in \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(Q)(S) = Q(S)\); this proves the existence of a \(q \in Q(S)\) with \(g = pq\). We have thus proved that the morphism considered in (ii) is covering for the étale topology. Comparing with 4.2.1 (ii), we deduce that it is smooth and surjective. On the other hand, an immediate argument shows that the equivalence relation defined in \(P \times_S Q\) by the morphism \(P \times_S Q \to G\) is the equivalence relation associated with the action of the group \(R = P \cap Q\) (acting as follows \((p, q)r = (pr, r^{-1}q)\)), which proves the last assertion of (ii) (since a smooth and surjective morphism is an effective epimorphism, for example).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 4.2.6

If \(P\) and \(Q\) are in transversal position, we shall often denote by \(P \cdot Q\) the open set \(\underline{\mathrm{Gen}}(Q/P)\) of \(G\), a notation justified by 4.2.5 (ii).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.2.7

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) and \(Q\) two parabolic subgroups of \(G\), the pair \((P, Q)\) being in transversal position.

(i) The group \(P \cap Q\) is smooth over \(S\) (and in fact with connected fibres by 4.1.2); let us then introduce \((P \cap Q)^0\) (cf. Exp. VIB); it is a subgroup of type (RC) of \(G\) (Exp. XXII, 5.11.1), whose unipotent radical (loc. cit. 5.11.4) decomposes into a direct product \[ \mathrm{rad}^u((P \cap Q)^0) = (\mathrm{rad}^u(P) \cap Q) \times_S (P \cap \mathrm{rad}^u(Q)). \]

(ii) If \(S\) is affine, \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, \mathrm{rad}^u(P \cap Q)^0) = 0\). If \(S\) is semi-local, \(P \cap Q\) contains a maximal torus of \(G\).
Indeed, \(P \cap Q\) is smooth by virtue of 4.2.1 (ii) and of the cartesian diagram \[ \xymatrix{ P \times_S Q \ar[r] & G \\ P \cap Q \ar[r] \ar@{^{(}->}[u] & S. \ar[u] } \]

To verify the assertions announced concerning \((P \cap Q)^0\), we may reason locally for the étale topology, and hence, by virtue of 4.2.1 (vii), assume that we have chosen a splitting \((G, T, M, R)\) of \(G\), such that \(P\) and \(Q\) contain \(T\) and are defined respectively by subsets \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) of \(R\), \(R_1\) containing a system of positive roots \(R_+\), and \(R_2\) containing the opposite system \(R_-\). Let \(R_0\) be the set of simple roots of \(R_+\); let us write \[ A_1 = R_0 \cap -R_1, \qquad A_2 = R_0 \cap R_1, \qquad A = A_1 \cap A_2. \] By 1.4 (v) and 1.12, we have \[ R_1 = R_+ \cup \big(R_- \cap -\mathbf{N}A_1\big), \qquad R_2 = \big(R_+ \cap \mathbf{N}A_2\big) \cup R_-, \] \[ \mathrm{rad}^u(P) = \prod_{\alpha \in R_1,\ \alpha \notin -R_1} U_\alpha, \qquad \mathrm{rad}^u(Q) = \prod_{\alpha \in R_2,\ \alpha \notin -R_2} U_\alpha. \]

By Exp. XXII, 5.6.7, we therefore have \[ \mathrm{rad}^u(P) \cap Q = \prod_{\alpha \in R_1 \cap R_2,\ \alpha \notin -R_1} U_\alpha = \prod_{\alpha \in K_2} U_\alpha, \] \[ \mathrm{rad}^u(Q) \cap P = \prod_{\alpha \in R_1 \cap R_2,\ \alpha \notin -R_2} U_\alpha = \prod_{\alpha \in K_1} U_\alpha, \] where \(K_2\) is the set of positive roots which are linear combinations of the elements of \(A_2\), but not linear combinations of the elements of \(A\), and \(K_1\) the set of negative roots which are linear combinations of the elements of \(A_1\), but not linear combinations of the elements of \(A\). It is clear that if \(\alpha \in K_2\), \(\beta \in K_1\), \(\alpha + \beta\) is never a root, nor zero, which entails that the two groups above commute.

On the other hand, we know by Exp. XXII, 5.4.5, that \(H = (P \cap Q)^0\) is defined by the set of roots \(R_1 \cap R_2\), that is \[ R_1 \cap R_2 = (R_+ \cap \mathbf{N}A_2) \cup (R_- \cap -\mathbf{N}A_1). \] Since \(R_1 \cap R_2\) is closed, \(H\) is of type (RC) by definition; by Exp. XXII, 5.11.3 and 5.11.4, we have \[ \mathrm{rad}^u(H) = \prod_{\alpha \in K} U_\alpha, \] where \(K\) is the set of \(\alpha \in R_1 \cap R_2\), with \(\alpha \notin -(R_1 \cap R_2)\). Since the symmetric part of \(R_1 \cap R_2\) is obviously \(R \cap \mathbf{Z}A\), one sees at once that \(K = K_1 \cup K_2\), which completes the proof of (i).

The first assertion of (ii) then follows from (i) and from 2.10; let us prove the second. Since \((P \cap Q)^0/\mathrm{rad}^u((P \cap Q)^0)\) is reductive, it possesses a maximal torus \(T\) if the base is semi-local. The inverse image of \(T\) in \((P \cap Q)^0\) is a subgroup \(H\) of type (R) of \(G\) with solvable fibres, and we have \(H^u = \mathrm{rad}^u((P \cap Q)^0)\) (Exp. XXII, 5.6.9). The scheme of maximal tori of \(H\) is a principal homogeneous bundle under \(H^u\) (loc. cit. 5.6.13), hence possesses a section, since \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, H^u) = 0\).
4.3. Opposite parabolic subgroups

If \(G\) is a reductive \(S\)-group, one has defined in Exp. XXIV, 3.16.6, a canonical "outer automorphism" \(s_G\) of order 2 of \(G\), hence a canonical automorphism of order 2 of \(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)\), hence likewise an automorphism of order 2 of \(\mathscr{B}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G))\), which we shall also denote by \(s_G\) or \(s\). Two types of parabolic subgroups \(t, t' \in \mathscr{B}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G))(S)\) will be called opposite when \(t = s_G(t')\).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 4.3.2

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\).

(a) If \(L\) is a Levi subgroup of \(P\), there exists a unique parabolic subgroup \(P'\) of \(G\) such that \(P \cap P' = L\).

(b) For every parabolic subgroup \(Q\) of \(G\), the following conditions are equivalent:

(i) For every \(s \in S\), \(((P \cap Q)_{\overline{s}})^0\) (which is smooth by 4.1.1) is reductive.

(ii) \(P \cap Q\) is a Levi subgroup of \(P\) and of \(Q\).

(iii) \(P\) and \(Q\) are of opposite types, and the pair \((P, Q)\) is in transversal position (cf. 4.2.3).

(iv) \(P\) and \(Q\) are of opposite types, \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P) \cap Q = e\).

(v) \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P) \cap Q = \mathrm{rad}^u(Q) \cap P = e\).

(vi) The canonical morphism \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P) \times_S Q \to G\) is an open immersion.

(vi′) The canonical morphism \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P) \to G/Q\) is an open immersion.

(vii) There exists a covering family for the étale topology \(\{S_i \to S\}\), and for each \(i\) a splitting \((T_i, M_i, R_i)\) of \(G_{S_i}\), and a subset \(R_i^{(1)}\) of \(R_i\) such that \(P_{S_i}\) (resp. \(Q_{S_i}\)) is the subgroup of type (R) of \(G_{S_i}\) containing \(T_i\) and defined by \(R_i^{(1)}\) (resp. by \(R_i^{(2)} = -R_i^{(1)}\)).

Proof. Let us first prove the second part of the theorem; one sees first of all that (iii) \(\Leftrightarrow\) (vii) by virtue of 4.2.1 (vii) and of the definition of \(s_G\) in the split case (Exp. XXII, 3.16.2 (iv)); we obviously have (ii) \(\Rightarrow\) (i); we have (vi′) \(\Rightarrow\) (vi) by base change \(G \to G/Q\).

Suppose now that (vii) is satisfied, and let us prove all the other conditions; since they are local for the étale topology, we may assume \(G = (G, T, M, R)\) split, \(P\) defined by the subset \(R'\) of \(R\) and \(Q\) by the subset \(-R'\). If \(L\) is the subgroup of type (R) of \(G\) containing \(T\) defined by \(R' \cap -R'\), it is clear by Exp. XXII, 5.11.3 that \(L\) is a Levi subgroup common to \(P\) and \(Q\). But \(P = L \cdot \mathrm{rad}^u(P)\), \(Q = L \cdot \mathrm{rad}^u(Q)\), and by Exp. XXII, 5.6.7, \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P) \cap Q = Q \cap \mathrm{rad}^u(P) = e\); hence \(P \cap Q = L\), and we have proved (ii) and (v). Since \(P\) and \(Q\) are in transversal position, the canonical morphism \(P \to G/Q\) induces an open immersion \(P/P \cap Q \to G/Q\) (4.2.1); but the canonical morphism \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P) \to P/P \cap Q = P/L\) is an isomorphism, so that we have proved (vi′). Taking account of what we have already seen, all the assertions are therefore consequences of (vii).

It now suffices for us to prove that any one whatever of the assertions (i), (iv), (v), (vi) implies (vii); since we have already proved the equivalence of (ii) and (iii), it suffices to carry out the proof on the geometric fibres and we may assume that \(S\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field. By 4.1.1, there exists a maximal torus \(T\) of \(G\) contained in \(P \cap Q\). Let \(R\) (resp. \(R_1\), resp. \(R_2\)) be the set of roots of \(G\) (resp. \(P\), resp. \(Q\)) relative to \(T\).

Let \(R_1^a\) be the asymmetric part of \(R_1\) (\(R_1^a = \{\alpha \in R_1,\ -\alpha \notin R_1\}\)). Let us introduce \(R_2^a\) in the same way. We must prove \(R'_1 = -R_2\). Condition (i) entails that \(R_1 \cap R_2\) is symmetric; let \(\alpha \in R_1\); if \(\alpha \notin R_2\), then \(\alpha \in -R_2\); if \(\alpha \in R_2\), then \(\alpha \in R_1 \cap R_2 = -(R_1 \cap R_2) \subset -R_2\); we therefore have \(R_1 \subset -R_2\), hence by symmetry \(R_1 = -R_2\). Condition (iv) entails \(\mathrm{Card}(R_1) = \mathrm{Card}(R_2)\), \(R_1^a \cap R_2 = \emptyset\); the second condition is equivalent to \(R_2 \subset -R_1\); the first then gives \(R_2 = -R_1\). Condition (v) entails \(R_1^a \cap R_2 = R_2^a \cap R_1 = \emptyset\), hence \(R_2 \subset -R_1\) and \(R_1 \subset -R_2\), which again gives \(R_2 = -R_1\). Condition (vi) entails \(\mathrm{Lie}(\mathrm{rad}^u(P)) \oplus \mathrm{Lie}(Q) = \mathrm{Lie}(G)\), which entails that \(R\) is the disjoint union of \(R_2\) and \(R_1^a\), hence that \(R_2 = -R_1\).

This completes the proof of the second part of the theorem. Let us prove the first; let us first remark that by virtue of (vii) \(\Rightarrow\) (ii), we have already proved the existence, locally for the étale topology, of the group \(P'\) sought; it therefore remains to prove its uniqueness, and this can likewise be done locally for the étale topology. We may therefore assume \(G\) split relative to a maximal torus \(T\) of \(L\), and \(P\) (resp. \(P'\)) defined by a subset \(R_1\) (resp. \(R'_1\)) of the system \(R\) of roots.
By hypothesis \(R_1 \cap R'_1\) is symmetric; reasoning as above, one deduces \(R'_1 = -R_1\), which proves that \(P'\) is determined by \(P\) and \(L\) and completes the proof.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 4.3.3

Two parabolic subgroups of \(G\) satisfying the equivalent conditions (i) to (vii) of 4.3.2 are said to be opposite.
