If \(P\) is a parabolic subgroup of \(G\), and if \(L\) is a Levi subgroup of \(P\) (resp. and if \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(P\)), one calls parabolic subgroup opposite to \(P\) relative to \(L\) (resp. \(T\)) the unique parabolic subgroup \(Q\) of \(G\) such that \(P \cap Q = L\) (resp. such that \(P \cap Q\) is the unique Levi subgroup of \(P\) containing \(T\), cf. 1.6, or again such that \(P \cap Q \subset T\) and that \(P\) and \(Q\) be opposite).
By virtue of 4.3.2 (iii), one deduces at once from 4.2.4 and 4.2.5 parallel results; let us give a sample of them.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.3.4

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) and \(Q\) two parabolic subgroups of \(G\).

(i) In order that \(P\) and \(Q\) be opposite, it is necessary and sufficient that for every point \(s \in S\), \(P_{\overline{s}}\) and \(Q_{\overline{s}}\) be opposite. If \(S' \to S\) is a surjective morphism, and if \(P_{S'}\) and \(Q_{S'}\) are opposite, then \(P\) and \(Q\) are opposite.

(ii) The functor \(\underline{\mathrm{Opp}}(G)\), such that for \(S' \to S\), \(\underline{\mathrm{Opp}}(G)(S')\) is the set of pairs of opposite parabolic subgroups of \(G_{S'}\), is representable by an open sub-prescheme of \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G)^2\). The functor \(\underline{\mathrm{Opp}}(/P)\) such that for \(S' \to S\), \(\underline{\mathrm{Opp}}(/P)(S')\) is the set of parabolic subgroups of \(G_{S'}\) opposite to \(P_{S'}\) is representable by a relatively dense open sub-prescheme of \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}_{s(\mathbf{t}(P))}(G)\).

(iii) Suppose \(P\) and \(Q\) opposite; let \(P'\) and \(Q'\) be two parabolic subgroups of \(G\), \(P'\) being of the same type as \(P\). In order that \(P'\) and \(Q'\) be opposite, it is necessary and sufficient that, locally for the étale topology, the pair \((P', Q')\) be conjugate to the pair \((P, Q)\). (N. B. We shall see in § 5 that the étale topology may be replaced by the Zariski topology).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.3.5

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\).

(i) The morphism \(\underline{\mathrm{Opp}}(/P) \to \underline{\mathrm{Lev}}(P)\) (cf. 1.9) defined set-theoretically by \(Q \mapsto P \cap Q\), is an isomorphism; \(\underline{\mathrm{Opp}}(/P)\) is a principal homogeneous bundle under \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P)\) (\(\mathrm{rad}^u(P)\) acting by inner automorphisms). If \(S\) is affine, there exists a parabolic subgroup of \(G\) opposite to \(P\).

(ii) Suppose \(S\) semi-local; let \(\{s_i\}\) be the set of its closed points; let, for each \(i\), \(Q_i\) be a parabolic subgroup of \(G_{s_i}\), opposite to \(P_{s_i}\). There exists a parabolic subgroup \(Q\) of \(G\), opposite to \(P\), and such that \(Q_{s_i} = Q_i\) for each \(i\).

(iii) The morphism \(\underline{\mathrm{Opp}}(G) \to \underline{\mathrm{PL}}\) (cf. 3.15) defined set-theoretically by \((P, Q) \mapsto (P, P \cap Q)\) is an isomorphism.
All this follows from the first part of the theorem and from 1.9, 2.3 and 2.8.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 4.3.6

Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be two opposite parabolic subgroups of \(G\). The "product morphism" \(G \times_S G \to G\) induces isomorphisms \[ \mathrm{rad}^u(P) \times_S Q \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } P \cdot Q \xleftarrow{\ \sim\ } P \times_S \mathrm{rad}^u(Q) \] \(P \cdot Q\) being the open sub-prescheme of \(G\), sheaf-theoretic image of \(P \times_S Q\), introduced in 4.2.6. This follows indeed from 4.3.2 (or from 4.2.5 (ii)) and from the fact that \(P \cap Q\) is a Levi subgroup of \(P\) and of \(Q\), so that \(P = \mathrm{rad}^u(P) \cdot P \cap Q\) and \(Q = \mathrm{rad}^u(Q) \cdot P \cap Q\).

We likewise have a commutative diagram \[ \xymatrix{ \mathrm{rad}^u(P) \ar@{^{(}->}[r] \ar[d]_{\wr} & G/Q \ar[d]^{\wr} \\ \underline{\mathrm{Opp}}(/P) \ar@{^{(}->}[r] & \underline{\mathrm{Par}}_{\mathbf{t}(Q)}(G), } \] where the vertical arrows are induced by \(g \mapsto \mathrm{int}(g)Q\).
4.4. Osculating position

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.4.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) and \(Q\) two parabolic subgroups of \(G\). The following conditions are equivalent:

(i) \(P \cap Q\) is a parabolic subgroup of \(G\).

(ii) \(P \cap Q\) contains, locally for the étale topology, a Borel group of \(G\).

(iii) \(P \cap Q\) contains, locally for the étale topology, a maximal torus of \(G\). For every \(S' \to S\) and every maximal torus \(T\) of \(G_{S'}\) contained in \(P_{S'}\) and \(Q_{S'}\), the opposite of \(P_{S'}\) relative to \(T\) is in transversal position relative to \(Q_{S'}\).

(iv) There exists a covering family for the étale topology \(\{S_i \to S\}\), and for each \(i\) a maximal torus \(T_i\) of \(G_{S_i}\) contained in \(P_{S_i}\) and \(Q_{S_i}\), and such that the opposite of \(P_{S_i}\) relative to \(T_i\) is in transversal position relative to \(Q_{S_i}\).

(v) There exists a covering family for the étale topology \(\{S_i \to S\}\), and for each \(i\) a splitting \((T_i, M_i, R_i)\) of \(G_{S_i}\) such that \(P_{S_i}\) (resp. \(Q_{S_i}\)) is the subgroup of type (R) of \(G_{S_i}\) containing \(T_i\) and defined by a set of roots \(R_i^{(1)}\) (resp. \(R_i^{(2)}\)), \(R_i^{(1)} \cap R_i^{(2)}\) containing a system of positive roots of \(R\).

Moreover, if these conditions are satisfied, we have \(\mathbf{t}(P \cap Q) = \mathbf{t}(P) \cap \mathbf{t}(Q)\) (with the notation of 3.2).

We have (v) \(\Rightarrow\) (ii) and (iii) \(\Rightarrow\) (iv) trivially. On the other hand, (ii) \(\Rightarrow\) (i) by 1.18. We have (iv) \(\Rightarrow\) (v): indeed, we may assume \(G\) split, \(P\) (resp. \(Q\)) defined by the set of roots \(R_1\) (resp. \(R_2\)); the opposite of \(P\) is then defined by \(-R_1\), and we are reduced to lemma 4.2.2. One proves (i) \(\Rightarrow\) (iii) by splitting in the same way. Finally, the last assertion of the theorem can be proved locally for the étale topology; we may assume that \(P \cap Q\) contains a Borel group \(B\) of \(G\) and we are reduced to 3.7.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 4.4.2

Two parabolic subgroups of \(G\) satisfying the conditions (i) to (v) of 4.4.1 are said to be in osculating position.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.4.3

Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be two parabolic subgroups in osculating position and let \(P'\) and \(Q'\) be two parabolic subgroups of \(G\), of the same type as \(P\) and \(Q\) respectively; in order that \(P'\) and \(Q'\) be in osculating position, it is necessary and sufficient that the pair \((P', Q')\) be conjugate to the pair \((P, Q)\), locally for the étale topology.

It suffices to prove that if \(P\) and \(P'\) are in osculating position with \(Q\), they are conjugate, locally for (ét), by a section of \(Q\). Now \(P \cap Q\) and \(P' \cap Q\) are two parabolic subgroups of the same type contained in \(Q\), hence are conjugate, locally for (ét), by a section of \(Q\), by virtue of part (ii) of the lemma below. We may therefore assume \(P \cap Q = P' \cap Q\); we then have \(P = P'\), by part (i) of the same lemma:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 4.4.4

Let \(P\), \(P'\) and \(Q\) be three parabolic subgroups of the reductive \(S\)-group \(G\).

(i) In order that \(P = P'\), it is necessary and sufficient that \(P\) and \(P'\) be in osculating position and of the same type.

(ii) If \(P \subset Q\), \(P' \subset Q\), and if \(g \in G(S)\) is such that \(\mathrm{int}(g)P\) and \(P'\) are in osculating position, then \(g \in Q(S)\).

Part (i) follows trivially from the last assertion of 4.4.1. Let us prove (ii): \(Q\) and \(\mathrm{int}(g)Q\) contain \(P' \cap \mathrm{int}(g)P\), hence are in osculating position; they coincide by (i), hence \(g \in \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(Q)(S) = Q(S)\).
Let us remark that assertions (iii) and (iv) of the theorem give at once:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.4.5

Let \(P\), \(P'\) and \(Q\) be three parabolic subgroups of the reductive \(S\)-group \(G\), containing the same maximal torus \(T\) of \(G\). Suppose \(P\) and \(P'\) opposite relative to \(T\). In order that \(Q\) be in osculating position relative to \(P\), it is necessary and sufficient that it be in transversal position relative to \(P'\). Under these conditions \(P \cap Q\) is also in transversal position relative to \(P'\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.4.6

Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be two parabolic subgroups of \(G\) containing the same maximal torus \(T\). In order that \(P\) and \(Q\) be in transversal position, it is necessary and sufficient that there exist two parabolic subgroups \(P'\) and \(Q'\) of \(G\), opposite relative to \(T\), and contained respectively in \(P\) and \(Q\). One may even choose \(\mathbf{t}(P') = \mathbf{t}(P) \cap s(\mathbf{t}(Q))\).

The condition is obviously sufficient (4.2.1 (i) and 4.3.2 (iii)). Let us show that it is necessary; let \(P^-\) (resp. \(Q^-\)) be the opposite of \(P\) (resp. \(Q\)) relative to \(T\). By 4.4.5, \(P^- \cap Q\) is in transversal position relative to \(P\) and \(Q^-\), hence also to \(P \cap Q^-\) by a fresh application of 4.4.5; moreover \[ \mathbf{t}(P^- \cap Q) = \mathbf{t}(P^-) \cap \mathbf{t}(Q) = s(\mathbf{t}(P)) \cap s(\mathbf{t}(Q^-)) = s(\mathbf{t}(P) \cap \mathbf{t}(Q^-)) = s(\mathbf{t}(P \cap Q^-)), \] hence \(P^- \cap Q = P'\) and \(P \cap Q^- = Q'\) are opposite (4.3.2 (iii)); but \(P' \cap Q' \supset T\), so they are indeed opposite relative to \(T\).
4.5. Standard position
In this no., we indicate briefly how some of the preceding results generalise.
If \(P\) and \(Q\) are two parabolic subgroups of the reductive \(S\)-group \(G\), the following conditions are equivalent:
(i) \(P \cap Q\) is smooth.
(ii) \(P \cap Q\) is a subgroup of type (R) (resp. of type (RC)) of \(G\).
(iii) \(P \cap Q\) contains, locally for the (fpqc) topology, a maximal torus of \(G\).
(iv) \(P \cap Q\) contains, locally for the Zariski topology, a maximal torus of \(G\).

When the preceding conditions are satisfied, one says that \(P\) and \(Q\) are in standard mutual position; this is for example the case if \(P\) and \(Q\) are in transversal position, or in osculating position, or if the base is the spectrum of a field. It is a notion stable under extension of the base and local for the (fpqc) topology.

Let \((P, Q)\) and \((P', Q')\) be two pairs of parabolic subgroups of \(G\), in standard position, and let \(H\) be the subfunctor of \(G\) defined as follows: \(H(S')\) is the set of \(g \in G(S')\) such that \(\mathrm{int}(g)P = P'\) and \(\mathrm{int}(g)Q = Q'\). It is a closed subprescheme of \(G\), smooth over \(S\) and formally principal homogeneous under \(P \cap Q\). One deduces from this that the following conditions are equivalent:
(i) \((P, Q)\) and \((P', Q')\) are conjugate locally for (fpqc),
(ii) \((P, Q)\) and \((P', Q')\) are conjugate locally for the étale topology.
(iii) \((P, Q)\) and \((P'Q')\) are conjugate on each geometric fibre.
One then says that the pairs \((P, Q)\) and \((P', Q')\) have the same type of mutual position. It is a notion stable under base change and local for the (fpqc) topology.

Let \(\underline{\mathrm{Stand}}(G)\) be the subfunctor of \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G) \times_S \underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G)\) "consisting of the pairs in standard mutual position". Then \(\underline{\mathrm{Stand}}(G)\) is representable, there exists an étale and finite \(S\)-prescheme \(\underline{\mathrm{TypeStand}}\) ("prescheme of the types of standard mutual position"), and a morphism, smooth, of finite presentation, with irreducible geometric fibres (hence in particular faithfully flat) \[ \mathbf{t}_2 : \underline{\mathrm{Stand}}(G) \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{TypeStand}} \] which is a quotient of \(\underline{\mathrm{Stand}}(G)\) by the action of \(G\): two sections of \(\underline{\mathrm{Stand}}(G)\) (over an arbitrary \(S' \to S\)) have the same type of mutual position if and only if they have the same image under \(\mathbf{t}_2\). One has a commutative diagram \[ \xymatrix{ \underline{\mathrm{Stand}}(G) \ar[r]^-{\mathbf{t}_2} \ar@{^{(}->}[d] & \underline{\mathrm{TypeStand}} \ar@{^{(}->}[d]^{q} \\ \underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G) \times_S \underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G) \ar[r]^-{\mathbf{t} \times \mathbf{t}} & \mathscr{B}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)) \times_S \mathscr{B}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G)), \\ } \] where the morphism \(q\) may be described by descent in the following way: if \((P, Q)\) is a pair of parabolic subgroups of \(G\) in standard relative position, and if \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(P \cap Q\), then the morphism \(\underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(T) \to \underline{\mathrm{Stand}}(G)\) defined set-theoretically by \(n \mapsto (P, \mathrm{int}(n)Q)\) induces an isomorphism \[ \mathrm{W}_P(T) \backslash \mathrm{W}_G(T) / \mathrm{W}_Q(T) \simeq q^{-1}(\mathbf{t}(P), \mathbf{t}(Q)). \] (The left-hand side denotes the sheaf of double cosets, \(\ldots\)). All these assertions are proved without difficulty (note in particular that \(\mathbf{t}_2^{-1}(\mathbf{t}_2(P, Q)) \simeq G/(P \cap Q)\)).

Let now \(P\) be a fixed parabolic subgroup of \(G\), and let \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G; P)\) be the functor of the parabolic subgroups of \(G\) in standard position relative to \(P\). For each \(t \in \mathscr{B}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G))(S)\), put likewise \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}_t(G; P) = \underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G; P) \cap \underline{\mathrm{Par}}_t(G)\). One sees at once that the two preceding functors are obtained from \(\underline{\mathrm{Stand}}(G)\) by fibre products, hence are representable by \(S\)-preschemes smooth and of finite presentation over \(S\), with non-empty fibres. One has a canonical morphism \(\mathbf{t}_P\) induced by \(\mathbf{t}_2\) (by \(\mathbf{t}_P(Q) = \mathbf{t}_2(P, Q)\)) \[ \mathbf{t}_P : \underline{\mathrm{Par}}_t(G; P) \longrightarrow q^{-1}(\mathbf{t}(P), t) \] which is smooth and of finite presentation, with irreducible geometric fibres. The canonical morphism \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}_t(G; P) \to \underline{\mathrm{Par}}_t(G)\) is a surjective monomorphism, and may therefore be regarded as a cellular decomposition of \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}_t(G)\) (indexed by the set of connected components of \(q^{-1}(\mathbf{t}(P), t)\)).

Suppose now that the type \(t\) is of the form \(\mathbf{t}(Q)\), where \(Q\) is a parabolic subgroup of \(G\) in standard position relative to \(P\), and that \(P \cap Q\) contains a maximal torus \(T\).

Then \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}_t(G) \simeq G/Q\), \(q^{-1}(\mathbf{t}(P), t) \simeq \mathrm{W}_P(T) \backslash \mathrm{W}_G(T) / \mathrm{W}_Q(T)\), which gives a diagram \[ \xymatrix{ \underline{\mathrm{Par}}_{\mathbf{t}(Q)}(G; P) \ar[r]^-{f} \ar@{^{(}->}[d]_{i} & \mathrm{W}_P(T) \backslash \mathrm{W}_G(T) / \mathrm{W}_Q(T) \\ \underline{\mathrm{Par}}_{\mathbf{t}(Q)}(G) \ar[r]^-{\sim} & G/Q \\ } \] where \(i\) is a surjective monomorphism, and where \(f\) is smooth and of finite presentation, with irreducible geometric fibres. Moreover, if \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) are two sections of \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}_{\mathbf{t}(Q)}(G; P)\) (over an \(S' \to S\)), that is to say two parabolic subgroups of \(G_{S'}\) conjugate (locally for (fpqc)) to \(Q\), and in standard position relative to \(P_{S'}\), then \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) are conjugate by a section of \(P\) (locally for (fpqc)) if and only if \(f(Q_1) = f(Q_2)\). If \(S\) is the spectrum of an algebraically closed field \(k\), one thus finds the relation \[ P(k) \backslash G(k) / Q(k) \simeq \mathrm{W}_P(T)(k) \backslash \mathrm{W}_G(T)(k) / \mathrm{W}_Q(T)(k). \] In general, if one supposes that the prescheme \(\mathrm{W}_P(T) \backslash \mathrm{W}_G(T) / \mathrm{W}_Q(T)\) is constant and of the form \(E_S\) (which happens for instance when \(G\) is split relative to \(T\) and \(S\) is connected), the \(f^{-1}(e)\), \(e \in E\), form a decomposition of \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}_{\mathbf{t}(Q)}(G; P)\) into open and closed subpreschemes, which are homogeneous spaces under \(P\), smooth and of finite presentation over \(S\), with irreducible geometric fibres.

Let us return to the general situation of 4.5.4. The prescheme \(t^{-1}(\mathbf{t}(P), t)\) always possesses two particular sections, corresponding respectively to the types "transversal position" and "osculating position". The inverse image of the first section is a relatively dense open subset of \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}_t(G)\), as was seen above; it is the cell of maximal relative dimension of the decomposition.
The inverse image of the second section is presumably a closed subprescheme of \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}_t(G)\); it is the cell of minimal relative dimension of the decomposition.
5. Conjugacy theorem

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.1

Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) and \(P'\) two opposite parabolic subgroups (4.3.3) of \(G\). Then \[ \mathrm{rad}^u(P)(S)\ P' \cdot P = G, \] i.e. the union of the open sets \(u P' \cdot P\) (4.3.6), for \(u\) running through \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P)(S)\), is all of \(G\).
The proof is carried out in several steps:
It suffices to give the proof in the case where \(S\) is the spectrum of a field \(k\); this follows at once from 2.6.

Let \(L = P \cap P'\). Suppose that \(L\) possesses a Borel group \(B_L\); let \(T\) be a maximal torus of \(B_L\) (Exp. XXII, 5.9.7); one verifies at once that \(B = B_L \cdot \mathrm{rad}^u(P)\) is a Borel group of \(P\); let \(B'\) be the Borel group of \(G\) opposite to \(B\) relative to \(T\) (i.e. such that \(B \cap B' = T\)). One has \(B' \subset P'\), as one verifies at once by splitting \(G\) relative to \(T\). Let us prove that \[ \mathrm{(x)} \qquad B^u(S)\ B' \cdot B \subset \mathrm{rad}^u(P)(S)\ P' \cdot P. \] Since one has \(B^u(S) \subset P(S) = \mathrm{rad}^u(P)(S) \cdot L(S) \subset \mathrm{rad}^u(P)(S)P'(S)\), it suffices to prove that \(B' \cdot B \subset P' \cdot P\), which is evident. It follows from (x) that it suffices to prove 5.1 for the pair \((B, B')\).
The theorem is true if \(k\) is algebraically closed; indeed, the condition of 5.1.2 is satisfied, and one concludes by Exp. XXII, 5.7.10.
The theorem is true when \(k\) is an infinite field. Indeed, \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P)(k)\) is dense in \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P)(\overline{k})\) by 2.7, and the theorem is true for \(\overline{k}\).

We are thus reduced to the case where \(k\) is a finite field. Now \(\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(L)\) is a smooth homogeneous space of \(L\); it therefore follows from LANG's theorem (Am. J. of Maths., 78, 1956) that \(L\) possesses a Borel group \(B_L\). By 5.1.2, we may therefore suppose that \(P = B\) and \(P' = B'\) are Borel groups. We write \(T = B \cap B'\).

Let \(K\) be the algebraic closure of \(k\); let us choose a pinning of the triple \((G_K, B_K, T_K)\), and let \(R_+\) (resp. \(R_0\)) be the set of positive (resp. simple) roots. By virtue of Exp. XXII, 5.7.2, it suffices to prove that for every \(\alpha \in R_0\) one has \[ \mathrm{(1)} \qquad u_\alpha\, B'^u(K) \subset B^u(k)\, B'^u(K)\, B(K). \] Let \(\alpha_i\) be the various roots conjugate to \(\alpha\) over \(k\) (they are elements of \(R_0\), since \(B\) is "defined over \(k\)"), and let \(R'\) be the set of roots that are linear combinations of the \(\alpha_i\). We write \(R'_- = R_- \cap R'\). Since "\(R'\) is defined over \(k\)", there exists a subtorus \(Q\) of \(T\) such that \(Q_K\) is the maximal torus of the common kernel of the \(\alpha_i\).

Let us write \(Z = \underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q)\), \(B_Z = B \cap Z\), \(B'_Z = B' \cap Z\) (cf. Exp. XXII, 5.10.2). Let us show that it suffices to verify the assertion in question in \(Z\), that is to say \[ \mathrm{(2)} \qquad u_\alpha \cdot B'^u_Z(K) \subset B^u_Z(k)\, B'^u_Z(K)\, B_Z(K). \] One has \((B'^u_Z)_K = \prod_{\alpha \in R'_-} U_\alpha\); let \(R''\) be the complement of \(R'\) in \(R\), and put \[ V = \prod_{\alpha \in R'' \cap R_-} U_\alpha. \]

One has at once \((B'^u)_K = (B'^u_Z)_K \cdot V\), and \((B_Z)_K\) normalises \(V\) (Exp. XXII, 5.6.7). One therefore deduces from (2) successively \[ \begin{aligned} u_\alpha \cdot B'^u(K) = u_\alpha \cdot B'^u_Z(K)\, V(K) &\subset B^u_Z(k)\, B'^u_Z(K)\, B_Z(K)\, V(K) \\ &\subset B^u_Z(k)\, B'^u_Z(K)\, V(K)\, B_Z(K) \end{aligned} \] which entails (1) at once.
We are thus reduced to the case where \(G = Z\), that is to say where the Galois group of \(K\) over \(k\) acts transitively on the simple roots.

The assertion to be proved is equivalent to the fact that \(G/B\) is the union of the translates of the open image of \(B'^u\) under \(B^u(k)\), an assertion which does not change if one replaces \(G\) by its adjoint group (or indeed by any group giving the same adjoint group). One may therefore suppose \(G\) adjoint.

Let us then consider the Dynkin diagram of \(G_K\). The Galois group acts transitively on this Dynkin diagram. But this Galois group has only cyclic quotients, and the Dynkin diagram has no cycles. It follows at once that this diagram is of type \(n\,\mathrm{A}_1\), \(n \geqslant 0\), or \(m\,\mathrm{A}_2\), \(m \geqslant 0\). Using the canonical decomposition of Exp. XXIV, 5.9, one may write \[ G = \prod_{\mathrm{D}/K} G_0, \] where \(\mathrm{D}\) is a finite \(K\)-scheme and \(G_0\) is either a torus, or of type \(\mathrm{A}_1\), or of type \(\mathrm{A}_2\).

By Exp. XXIV, 5.12, \(B\) comes from a Borel group \(B_0\) of \(G_0\), and \(T\) from a maximal torus \(T_0\) of \(G_0\); \(B'\) comes from the Borel group \(B'_0\) of \(G_0\) opposite to \(B_0\) relative to \(T_0\). One has \[ B'^u(k) = B_0^u(\mathrm{D}), \] \[ B'^u \cdot T \cdot B^u = \prod_{\mathrm{D}/k} B'^u_0 \cdot T_0 \cdot B_0^u, \] and it suffices for us to prove the assertion in question for the triple \((G_0, B_0, T_0)\).

One may therefore suppose that \(G\) is of type \(0\), \(\mathrm{A}_1\) or \(\mathrm{A}_2\). Since \(G\) possesses a Borel group \(B\), \(G\) is quasi-splittable relative to \(B\) (Exp. XXIV, 3.9.1), hence splittable if it is of type \(0\) or \(\mathrm{A}_1\). As the theorem has already been proved in the split case (Exp. XXII 5.7.10), only the case \(\mathrm{A}_2\) remains to be treated. By Exp. XXIV, 3.11 there exists a morphism \(E \to \mathrm{Spec}(k)\), a Galois principal bundle under the group \(\mathbf{Z}/2\mathbf{Z}\) of automorphisms of the Dynkin diagram of type \(\mathrm{A}_2\), such that \(G = \text{Q-Ép}_{E/\mathrm{Spec}(k)}(\mathrm{A}_2)\). If \(E\) possesses a section, \(G\) is splittable and the theorem is proved. Otherwise, one necessarily has \(E = \mathrm{Spec}(k')\), where \(k'\) is a quadratic extension of \(k\). Finally, as was seen in 5.1.7, one may suppose \(G\) simply connected (i.e. a form of \(\mathrm{SL}_{3,\,k}\)).

We are thus in the following situation: we have a finite field \(k\) and a quadratic extension \(k'\) of \(k\). The group \(\mathrm{SL}_{3,\,k'}\) of \(3 \times 3\) matrices of determinant 1 is pinned as follows: the maximal torus is the group of diagonal matrices, the Borel group is the group of upper triangular matrices, and the "pinnings" are the elements: \[ u_\alpha = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \qquad \text{and} \qquad = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. \] One sees at once that the big cell \(\Omega\) is defined by \[ x = \begin{pmatrix} a & b & c \\ d & e & f \\ g & h & i \end{pmatrix} \in \Omega(S) \Longleftrightarrow a \text{ and } ae - bd \text{ invertible}, \] and that \[ B^u(k) = \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \overline{x} & z \\ 0 & 1 & x \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \ \middle|\ \ x, z \in k', \quad z + \overline{z} = x\overline{x} \right\}. \]

We must prove the inclusion (1), that is to say show that for all \(a\), \(b\), \(c \in K\) (the algebraic closure of \(k\)) there exist \(x, z \in k'\), with \(z + \overline{z} = x\overline{x}\), such that \[ \mathrm{(1)} \qquad \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \overline{x} & z \\ 0 & 1 & x \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ a & 1 & 0 \\ b & c & 1 \end{pmatrix} \subset \Omega_{(K)}. \]
– If \(a \neq -1\), one takes \(x = z = 0\).

– If \(a = -1\), the conditions to be met are written \[ \begin{cases} z + \overline{z} = x\overline{x}, \\ bz - \overline{x} \neq 0, \\ (b + c)\overline{z} + bx - 1 \neq 0. \end{cases} \] Let \(q\) be the number of elements of \(k\) (\(q \geqslant 2\)). It is known that for every \(m \in k\), the equation \(z + \overline{z} = m\), with \(z \in k'\), has \(q\) solutions.
– If \(b = 0\), let us take \(x = 1\); one must solve \(z + \overline{z} = 1\), \(c\overline{z} \neq 1\), which is always possible by the preceding remark.

– If \(b eq 0\), let us take \(x = 0\); one must solve \[ z + \overline{z} = 0, \qquad z eq 0, \qquad (b + c)\overline{z} eq 1. \] This is always possible if \(q \geqslant 3\). If \(k = \mathbf{F}_2\), it is possible if \(b + c eq 1\): one may take \(z = 1\).

– There thus remains to be treated only the case \(k = \mathbf{F}_2\), \(b + c = 1\), \(b eq 0\). The system is then written \[ z + \overline{z} = x\overline{x}, \qquad bz eq \overline{x}, \qquad \overline{z} + bx eq 1. \] If \(b = 1\) (resp. \(b otin k'\)), let us put \(x = 1\); then the last two conditions are written \(z eq b^{-1}, 1 - b\), and they are consequences of \(z + \overline{z} = 1\), which has solutions.
Finally, if \(b \in k'\), \(b \notin k\), one may take \(x = \overline{b}\), \(z = b\). Q.E.D.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.2

Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) and \(P'\) two opposite parabolic subgroups of \(G\). The canonical map \[ \mathrm{rad}^u(P)(S) \cdot \mathrm{rad}^u(P')(S) \longrightarrow (G/P)(S) \] is surjective (in particular, one has \((G/P)(S) = G(S)/P(S)\)). Every parabolic subgroup \(Q\) of \(G\) of the same type as \(P\) is of the form \(\mathrm{int}(uu')P\) with \(u \in \mathrm{rad}^u(P)(S)\) and \(u' \in \mathrm{rad}^u(P')(S)\).

The second assertion is evidently equivalent to the first; let us prove the latter. Let \(s_i\) be the closed points of \(S\), let \(V\) be the open subset of \(G/P\) which is the image of \(P'\) (and isomorphic to \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P')\), cf. 4.3.6), and let \(x \in G/P(S)\). By 5.1, there exists for each \(i\) a section \(u_i \in \mathrm{rad}^u(P)(k(s_i))\) such that \(u_i x_{s_i}\) is a section of \(V_{s_i}\). If \(u \in \mathrm{rad}^u(P)(S)\) lifts the \(u_i\) (2.6), then \(ux\) is a section of \(V\), for such an assertion is verified on the closed fibres. But \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P')(S) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } V(S)\) is bijective, and one concludes at once.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.3

Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\), \(P'\) and \(Q\) three parabolic subgroups of \(G\). There exists \(g \in G(S)\) such that \(\mathrm{int}(g)Q\) is in transversal position relative to \(P\) and \(P'\).

With the notation of 4.2.4 (ii), one must verify that the relatively dense open subset \(\underline{\mathrm{Gen}}(Q/P) \cap \underline{\mathrm{Gen}}(Q/P')\) of \(G\) possesses a section over \(S\). In fact, let us choose a parabolic subgroup of \(G\) opposite to \(Q\) (4.3.5 (i)), say \(Q_1\), and put \(U = \mathrm{rad}^u(Q)\), \(U' = \mathrm{rad}^u(Q_1)\). We are going to show that there exists \(g \in U(S)U'(S)\) answering the question; in this form, it follows from 4.2.4 (i) and 2.6 that it suffices to verify the assertion on the fibres at the closed points of \(S\), and one may therefore suppose that \(S\) is the spectrum of a field \(k\).

If \(k\) is algebraically closed, there exists \(g \in G(k)\) answering the question, but \(g\) is written \(uu'q\) with \(u \in U(k)\), \(u' \in U'(k)\), \(q \in Q(k)\) (5.1), and \(\mathrm{int}(uu')Q = \mathrm{int}(g)Q\).

If \(k\) is infinite, let us consider the open subset \(V\) of \(U \times_k U'\) defined by the cartesian diagram \[ \xymatrix{ U \times_k U' \ar[r] & G \\ V \ar[r] \ar@{^{(}->}[u] & \underline{\mathrm{Gen}}(Q/P) \cap \underline{\mathrm{Gen}}(Q/P'); \ar@{^{(}->}[u] } \] since \(V(\overline{k}) \neq \emptyset\) by virtue of what we have just seen, \(V\) is dense in \(U \times_k U'\), hence possesses a section by 2.7.

If \(k\) is finite, \(P\) (resp. \(P'\)) possesses a Borel group \(B\) (resp. \(B'\)), by virtue of Lang's theorem (cf. 5.1.5), the schemes \(\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(P) \simeq \underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(P/\mathrm{rad}^u(P))\) and \(\underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(Q) \simeq \underline{\mathrm{Bor}}(Q/\mathrm{rad}^u(Q))\) being smooth. If \(B_1\) is a Borel subgroup opposite to \(B\) (4.3.5 (i)), there exist \(a \in B^u(k)\) and \(a_1 \in B_1^u(k)\) with \(\mathrm{int}(aa_1)B = B'\) (5.2); then \(B_0 = \mathrm{int}(aa_1)B_1 = \mathrm{int}(a)B_1\) is opposite to \(B'\) and to \(B\); if \(Q_0\) is the unique parabolic subgroup of \(G\) containing \(B_0\) and of the same type as \(Q\) (3.8), then \(Q_0\) is in transversal position relative to \(P\) and \(P'\) (4.2.1 (vi)). On the other hand, by 5.2, \(Q_0\) is written \(\mathrm{int}(uu')Q\) with \(u' \in U'(k)\), \(u \in U(k)\), which is what had to be proved.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.4

Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) and \(Q\) two parabolic subgroups of \(G\). There exists \(g \in G(S)\) such that \(\mathrm{int}(g)P\) is in osculating position relative to \(Q\), i.e. (4.4.2) such that \(\mathrm{int}(g)P \cap Q\) is a parabolic subgroup of \(G\).

Indeed, by virtue of 4.3.5 (i), there exists a parabolic subgroup \(P'\) of \(G\) opposite to \(P\). By virtue of 5.3, there exists a parabolic subgroup \(P'_1\) of \(G\) of the same type as \(P'\), in transversal position relative to \(P\) and \(Q\). If \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(P'_1 \cap Q\) (4.2.7 (ii)), and if \(P_1\) is the opposite of \(P'_1\) relative to \(T\), then \(P_1\) and \(Q\) are in osculating position, by virtue of 4.4.5. On the other hand, \(P\) and \(P_1\) being opposite to \(P'_1\), there exists \(g \in \mathrm{rad}^u(P'_1)(S)\) with \(\mathrm{int}(g)P = P_1\) (4.3.5 (i)). Q.E.D.

Let us remark, moreover, that for the same reason there exists \(u \in \mathrm{rad}^u(P)(S)\) with \(\mathrm{int}(u)P' = P'_1\), so that \(g\) is written \(\mathrm{int}(u)u'\) with \(u' \in \mathrm{rad}^u(P')(S)\), which gives \(P_1 = \mathrm{int}(uu'u^{-1})P = \mathrm{int}(uu')P\) and reproves 5.2 in passing.
The statements 5.3 and above all 5.4 are the essential results of this section. Let us first state a few consequences of 5.4.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.5

Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group.

(i) If \(P\) and \(Q\) are two parabolic subgroups of \(G\) and if \(\mathbf{t}(P) \subset \mathbf{t}(Q)\) (cf. 3.3), there exists \(g \in G(S)\) such that \(\mathrm{int}(g)P \subset Q\).

(ii) Let \[ P_1 \supset P_2 \supset \cdots\cdots \supset P_n \qquad \text{and} \qquad P'_1 \supset P'_2 \supset \cdots\cdots \supset P'_n \] be two chains of parabolic subgroups of \(G\) such that \(\mathbf{t}(P_i) = \mathbf{t}(P'_i)\). There exists \(g \in G(S)\) such that \(\mathrm{int}(g)P_i = P'_i\) for each \(i\).

(iii) Let \(P\), \(Q\), \(P'\), \(Q'\) be four parabolic subgroups of \(G\), with \(\mathbf{t}(P) = \mathbf{t}(P')\), \(\mathbf{t}(Q) = \mathbf{t}(Q')\). If the pairs \((P, P')\) and \((Q, Q')\) are in transversal (resp. osculating) position, there exists \(g \in G(S)\) with \(\mathrm{int}(g)P = P'\), \(\mathrm{int}(g)Q = Q'\).

(iv) Let \(P\) and \(P'\) be two parabolic subgroups of the same type, and \(L\) (resp. \(L'\)) a Levi subgroup of \(P\) (resp. \(P'\)). There exists \(g \in G(S)\) with \(\mathrm{int}(g)P = P'\), \(\mathrm{int}(g)L = L'\).

Proof: (i) follows at once from 5.4; (ii) is proved by induction on \(n\), the case \(n = 0\) being trivial; one may therefore suppose \(P_i = P'_i\) for \(i = 1, \ldots, n-1\); by 5.2 there exists \(g \in G(S)\) with \(\mathrm{int}(g)P_n = P'_n\); but then \(P_n\) and \(\mathrm{int}(g)P_n\) are contained in \(P_{n-1} = P'_{n-1}\), hence \(g \in P_{n-1}(S)\) (4.4.4 (ii)) and \(\mathrm{int}(g)P_i = P'_i\) for \(i = 1, \ldots, n\).

On the other hand, (iv) follows at once from 5.2 and 1.8. Let us prove (iii) in the case of "transversal position"; the assertion is a consequence of (iv) when the types of \(P\) and \(Q\) are opposite (4.3.3 (iii)); in the general case one may, by virtue of 4.2.7 (iii) and 4.4.6, find parabolic subgroups \(P_1\), \(P'_1\), \(Q_1\), \(Q'_1\) of \(P\), \(P'\), \(Q\), \(Q'\) respectively, such that \(P_1\) and \(P'_1\) are opposite, as are \(Q_1\) and \(Q'_1\), and such that \(\mathbf{t}(P_1) = \mathbf{t}(P'_1)\); there exists therefore \(g \in G(S)\) with \(\mathrm{int}(g)P_1 = P'_1\), \(\mathrm{int}(g)Q_1 = Q'_1\), and one may suppose \(P_1 = P'_1\) and \(Q_1 = Q'_1\); but then \(P\) and \(P'\) are in osculating position and of the same type, hence \(P = P'\) (4.4.4 (i)); for the same reason \(Q = Q'\).

It remains for us to prove assertion (iii) in the case of "osculating position". By virtue of the conjugacy theorem (5.2), one may suppose \(P = P'\); by virtue of the same theorem, one may find \(g \in G(S)\) with \(\mathrm{int}(g)Q = Q'\); but then \(g \in P(S)\) by 4.4.4 (ii) and \(\mathrm{int}(g)P = P = P'\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 5.6

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\). One says that \(P\) is minimal if, whenever \(G\) is a parabolic subgroup of \(G\) contained in \(P\), one has \(Q = P\).
It will be noted that this is not in general a notion stable under passage to the fibres.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.7

Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group.

(i) Let \(t, t' \in \mathscr{B}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G))(S)\). If there exist in \(G\) a parabolic subgroup of type \(t\) and a parabolic subgroup of type \(t'\), there exists a parabolic subgroup of type \(t \cap t'\). In particular, there exists a smallest element \(t_{\min}\) in the set of the \(\mathbf{t}(P)\), \(P\) running through the set of parabolic subgroups of \(G\).

(ii) Every parabolic subgroup of \(G\) contains a minimal parabolic subgroup. For a parabolic subgroup of \(G\) to be minimal, it is necessary and sufficient that it be of type \(t_{\min}\). Two minimal parabolic subgroups of \(G\) are conjugate by an element of \(G(S)\).
This follows at once from 5.4 and 5.5 (i).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.8

A parabolic subgroup opposite to a minimal parabolic subgroup is likewise minimal; this entails \(s(t_{\min}) = t_{\min}\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.9

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\). The canonical morphism \[ G \longrightarrow G/P = X \] makes \(G\) an \(X\)-bundle, locally trivial (in the Zariski sense), with group \(P_X\). If \(L\) is a Levi group of \(P\), the canonical morphism (cf. 3.12) \[ G \longrightarrow G/L = Y \] makes \(G\) a \(Y\)-bundle, locally trivial (in the Zariski sense), with group \(L_Y\).

It suffices to prove that if one has a morphism \(S' \to S\), where \(S'\) is local, and a morphism \(S' \to X\) (resp. \(S' \to Y\)), the latter lifts to a morphism \(S' \to G\). In other words, one may suppose \(S\) local, and one must show that \(G(S) \to X(S)\) (resp. \(G(S) \to Y(S)\)) is surjective.

The first assertion was proved in 5.2; let us prove the second. Let \(y \in Y(S)\); its canonical image in \(X(S)\) comes from a \(g \in G(S)\); the projection \(y'\) of \(g\) in \(Y(S)\) therefore has the same projection as \(y\) in \(X(S)\). There exists therefore a unique \(u \in \mathrm{rad}^u(P)(S)\) with \(y'u = y\), and the projection of \(gu\) in \(Y(S)\) is indeed \(y\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.10

Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group

(i) Let \(P\) be a parabolic subgroup of \(G\), and \(L\) a Levi subgroup of \(P\). The canonical maps (cf. 3.21) induce bijections \[ \mathrm{H}^1(S, L) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{H}^1(S, P) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{H}^1_{\mathbf{t}(P)}(S, G). \]

(ii) Let \(t, t' \in \mathscr{B}(\underline{\mathrm{Dyn}}(G))(S)\); one has (cf. 3.21) \[ \mathrm{H}^1_t(S, G) \bigcap \mathrm{H}^1_{t'}(S, G) = \mathrm{H}^1_{t \cap t'}(S, G). \]

(iii) If \(P\) and \(Q\) are two parabolic subgroups of \(G\) in osculating position, the following canonical diagram is cartesian and composed of injections: \[ \xymatrix{ \mathrm{H}^1(S, P) \ar[r] & \mathrm{H}^1(S, G) \\ \mathrm{H}^1(S, P \cap Q) \ar[r] \ar[u] & \mathrm{H}^1(S, Q). \ar[u] } \]

Let us prove (i). The map \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, L) \to \mathrm{H}^1(S, P)\) is bijective by 2.3; the map \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, P) \to \mathrm{H}^1_{\mathbf{t}(P)}(S, G)\) is surjective (3.21); let us show that it is injective, i.e. that the canonical map \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, P) \to \mathrm{H}^1(S, G)\) is injective. Let \(Q\) be a principal bundle under \(P\), \(Q_1\) the associated principal bundle under \(G\), and \(P'\) and \(G'\) the corresponding twisted forms of \(P\) and \(G\). It is clear that \(G'\) is a reductive \(S\)-group and that \(P'\) is a parabolic subgroup of it. The set of elements of \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, P)\) having the same image as the class of \(Q\) in \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, G)\) is naturally identified with the kernel of the canonical map \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, P') \to \mathrm{H}^1(S, G')\), and the latter, by the exact cohomology sequence, with the set of orbits of \(G'(S)\) in \((G'/P')(S)\) (For these arguments of non-abelian cohomology, see GIRAUD's thesis). But \(G'(S)\) acts transitively on \((G'/P')(S)\) by 5.2.

Let us prove (ii): let \(Q\) be a principal homogeneous bundle under \(G\) and \(G^Q\) the corresponding twisted form of \(G\). By definition (3.21), we must prove that \(G^Q\) possesses a parabolic subgroup of type \(t \cap t'\) if and only if it possesses parabolic subgroups of type \(t\) and \(t'\), which is nothing other than the conjunction of 3.8 and 5.7 (i).
Finally, (iii) follows at once from (i) and (ii).
Let us now state a consequence of 5.3.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.11

Let \(S\) be a semi-local scheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\). If \(P \neq G\), there exist at least three distinct parabolic subgroups of \(G\) of the same type as \(P\); in other words \(P \neq G\) entails \((G(S) : P(S)) \geqslant 3\).

Indeed, let \(P'\) be a parabolic subgroup of \(G\) opposite to \(P\) (4.3.5 (i)). Since \(P eq G\), one has \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P') eq e\) (by 4.3.2 for example). By 2.1, \(\mathrm{rad}^u(P')(S') eq e\); let therefore \(u \in \mathrm{rad}^u(P')(S')\), \(u eq e\). Then \(\mathrm{int}(u)P eq P\), and by virtue of 5.3 there exists a \(P_1\), of the same type as \(P\), opposite to \(P\) and to \(\mathrm{int}(u)P\); then \(P_1\), \(P\) and \(\mathrm{int}(u)P\) are three distinct parabolic subgroups of \(G\) of the same type as \(P\).
6. Parabolic subgroups and trivial tori

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.1

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(Q\) a trivial subtorus of \(G\). Let us write \(Q = \mathrm{D}_S(M)\) and let \[ \mathfrak{g} = \coprod_{m \in M} \mathfrak{g}^m \] be the decomposition of the Lie algebra of \(G\) under the action of \(Q\). Let \(M_1\) be a subset of \(M\) such that \(0 \in M_1\) and \(x, y \in M_1 \Rightarrow x + y \in M_1\).

(i) There exists a unique smooth subgroup \(\mathrm{H}_{M_1}\) of \(G\), with connected fibres, containing \(\underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q)\), and whose Lie Algebra is \(\coprod_{m \in M_1} \mathfrak{g}^m\).

(ii) We have the following implications: \[ \begin{aligned} M_1 = \{0\} &\Longrightarrow \mathrm{H}_{M_1} = \underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q), \\ M_1 = -M_1 &\Longrightarrow \mathrm{H}_{M_1} \text{ is reductive}, \\ M_1 \cup (-M_1) = M &\Longrightarrow \mathrm{H}_{M_1} \text{ and } \mathrm{H}_{-M_1} \text{ are parabolic subgroups of } G, \\ &\hphantom{\Longrightarrow{}} \text{opposite, whose common Levi group is } \mathrm{H}_{M_1 \cap -M_1}. \end{aligned} \]

To prove (i) and (ii), which are local for the (fpqc) topology, we may assume that \(Q\) is contained in a maximal torus \(T\) of \(G\); we may moreover split \(G\) relatively to \(T\). Assertion (i) then follows at once from Exp. XXII, 5.3.5, 5.4.5 and 5.4.7; the assertions of (ii) follow from Exp. XXII, 5.3.5, 5.10.1, 5.11.3 and from this exposé, 1.4, 4.3.2.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.2

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(Q\) a trivial subtorus of \(G\). There exists a parabolic subgroup of \(G\) of which \(\underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q)\) is a Levi subgroup.

Indeed, writing \(Q = \mathrm{D}_S(M)\), one chooses a total order structure on the group \(M\) and lets \(M_1\) be the set of positive elements of \(M\); the group \(\mathrm{H}_{M_1}\) answers the question.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.3

If the reductive \(S\)-group \(G\) possesses a non-central trivial subtorus, it possesses a proper parabolic subgroup (i.e. \(\neq G\)).
By 5.9 and 5.10, one deduces from 6.2:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.4

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(Q\) a trivial subtorus of \(G\). The canonical morphism \(G \to G/\underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q)\) is a locally trivial fibration.

If \(S\) is semi-local, the map \(G(S) \to (G/\underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q))(S)\) is surjective, and the map \(\mathrm{H}^1(S, \underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q)) \to \mathrm{H}^1(S, G)\) is injective.

Suppose \(S\) connected. If \(T\) is an \(S\)-torus and if \(T'\) and \(T''\) are two trivial subtori of \(T\), their sum \(T' + T''\) is likewise a trivial subtorus of \(T\). Indeed it is identified with the quotient of \(T' \times_S T''\) by \(T' \cap T''\), a quotient which is trivial by Exp. IX, 2.11. It follows that \(T\) possesses a largest trivial subtorus; we denote it by \(T_{\text{dép}}\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.6

Let \(S\) be a connected prescheme, \(T\) an isotrivial \(S\)-torus, \(T_{\text{dép}}\) its largest trivial subtorus. The following conditions are equivalent:

(i) There exists a homomorphism \(T \to \mathbf{G}_{m,\,S}\) distinct from \(e\).

(ii) \(T_{\text{dép}} \neq e\).

Since \(T\) is assumed isotrivial, there exist a finite group \(G\), a connected Galois principal covering \(S' \to S\) with group \(G\), and an isomorphism \(T_{S'} \simeq \mathrm{D}_{S'}(M)\); \(M\) is then endowed with a structure of \(G\)-module, and one has a natural isomorphism \(\mathrm{Hom}_S(T, \mathbf{G}_{m,\,S}) = \mathrm{H}^0(G, M)\).

On the other hand, let \(V\) be the vector subspace of \(M \otimes \mathbf{Q}\) generated by the elements of the form \(g(m) - m\), \(g \in G\), \(m \in M\). One checks at once that \((T_{ ext{dép}})_{S'}\) is identified with \(\mathrm{D}_{S'}(M/M \cap V)\). Assertion (i) is therefore equivalent to \(\mathrm{H}^0(G, M) eq 0\), or again to \(\mathrm{H}^0(G, M \otimes \mathbf{Q}) eq 0\), while assertion (ii) is equivalent to \(M eq M \cap V\), or again to \(M \otimes \mathbf{Q} eq V\). Now one has \(M \otimes \mathbf{Q} = \mathrm{H}^0(G, M \otimes \mathbf{Q}) \oplus V\), as one checks at once (consider the projector \(M \otimes \mathbf{Q} o \mathrm{H}^0(G, M \otimes \mathbf{Q})\) which sends \(x\) to the average of the transforms of \(x\) under \(G\)).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.7

Let \(S\) be a prescheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\) such that \(P \neq G\), \(L\) a Levi subgroup of \(P\), \(Q\) its radical. There exists a homomorphism \(Q \to \mathbf{G}_{m,\,S}\) distinct from \(e\).

Consider the unipotent radical \(U\) of \(P\); it is invariant under \(\mathrm{int}(P)\), hence under \(\mathrm{int}(Q)\). Consider the invertible \(\mathscr{O}_S\)-Module \(\operatorname{d\acute{e}t}(\mathrm{Lie}(U))\), the "maximum exterior power" of the locally free \(\mathscr{O}_S\)-Module \(\mathrm{Lie}(U)\). The adjoint representation defines a homomorphism of groups \[ f : \quad Q \longrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Aut}}(\operatorname{d\acute{e}t}(\mathrm{Lie}(U)) = \mathbf{G}_{m,\,S}. \] If \(P eq G\), then \(U eq e\). Let us choose an \(s \in S\) such that \(U_s eq e\). Splitting \(G_{\overline{s}}\) relatively to a maximal torus containing \(Q_{\overline{s}}\), one sees at once that \(f_{\overline{s}} eq e\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.8

Let \(S\) be a connected semi-local scheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(P\) a parabolic subgroup of \(G\), \(L\) a Levi subgroup of \(P\), \(Q\) its radical, \(Q_{\text{dép}}\) the largest trivial subtorus of \(Q\) (i.e. the largest trivial central subtorus of \(L\)). Then \[ L = \underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q_{\text{dép}}). \]

Set \(L' = \underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q_{ ext{dép}})\); it is a reductive subgroup of \(G\) containing \(L\); moreover, \(P' = P \cap L'\) is a parabolic subgroup of \(L'\), with Levi subgroup \(L\) (1.20). If \(L' eq L\), then \(L' ot\subset P\) (for \(L\) is a maximal reductive subgroup of \(P\), cf. 1.7), hence \(P' eq L'\).

Let \(G_1\) be the derived group of \(G\), and \(P_1 = P' \cap G_1\). By 1.19, \(P_1\) is a parabolic subgroup of the semi-simple group \(G_1\), \(L_1 = L \cap G_1\) is a Levi subgroup of it, and \[ Q_1 = \mathrm{rad}(L_1) = (\mathrm{rad}(L) \cap G_1)^0 = (Q \cap G_1)^0. \] Since \(L_1\) possesses a maximal torus \(T_1\) (Exp. XXIV, 3.20), and since the latter is isotrivial (Exp. XXIV, 4.1.5), \(Q_1\), which is a subtorus of \(T_1\), is likewise isotrivial (Exp. IX, 2.11); since \(P_1 eq G_1\), one may apply 6.7 and 6.6 and \((Q_1)_{ ext{dép}} eq e\), hence \((Q_{ ext{dép}} \cap G_1)^0 eq e\), hence \(Q_{ ext{dép}} ot\subset \mathrm{rad}(L')\) (for \(\mathrm{rad}(L') \cap G_1\) is finite), which contradicts the definition of \(L'\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.9

Let \(S\) be a connected semi-local scheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(Q\) a critical subtorus of \(G\) (i.e. such that \(\mathrm{rad}(\underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q)) = Q\)). For \(\underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q)\) to be a Levi subgroup of a parabolic subgroup of \(G\), it is necessary and sufficient that \(\underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q) = \underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q_{\text{dép}})\), that is to say that \(\mathrm{Lie}(G)^Q = \mathrm{Lie}(G)^{Q_{\text{dép}}}\).
This follows from 6.2 and 6.8.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.10

Let \(S\) be a connected semi-local scheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(L\) a subgroup of \(G\). The following conditions are equivalent:

(i) There exists a parabolic subgroup of \(G\) of which \(L\) is a Levi subgroup.

(ii) There exists a trivial subtorus of \(G\) of which \(L\) is the centralizer.

(iii) There exists a homomorphism \(\mathbf{G}_{m,\,S} \to G\) of which \(L\) is the centralizer.

Indeed, one has (i) \(\Rightarrow\) (ii) by 6.8, (iii) \(\Rightarrow\) (i) by 6.1: it remains to prove (ii) \(\Rightarrow\) (iii); one may assume \(S\) connected, hence \(L = \underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q)\), with \(Q = \mathrm{D}_S(M)\); let us write \[ \mathrm{Lie}(G) = \coprod_{m \in M} \mathrm{Lie}(G)^m, \] and let \(R\) be the set of \(m \in M - \{0\}\) such that \(\mathrm{Lie}(G)^m \neq 0\).

Since \(R\) is finite and does not contain \(0\), there exists a homomorphism \(u : M \to \mathbf{Z}\) such that \(u(\alpha) \neq 0\) for every \(\alpha \in R\). By duality, \(u\) gives a homomorphism \(\mathbf{G}_{m,\,S} \to Q\), hence a homomorphism \(f : \mathbf{G}_{m,\,S} \to G\). One has \(\underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(f) \supset \underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q)\); these are two smooth subgroups of \(G\), with connected fibres; their Lie Algebras coincide (being both equal to \(\mathfrak{g}^0\)); they therefore coincide, by the usual argument.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.11

Let \(S\) be a connected semi-local scheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group. The maps \[ L \mapsto \mathrm{rad}(L)_{\text{dép}}, \qquad Q \mapsto \underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q) \] are mutually inverse bijections, which reverse the natural order structures, between the set of subgroups \(L\) of \(G\) which are Levi subgroups of parabolic subgroups of \(G\) and the set of trivial subtori of \(G\) such that \(\mathrm{rad}(\underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q))_{\text{dép}} = Q\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.12

Let \(S\) be a connected semi-local scheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group. Consider the following assertions:

(i) There exists a parabolic subgroup of \(G\) distinct from \(G\).

(ii) \(G\) possesses a non-central trivial subtorus.

(ii bis) \(G\) possesses a non-central trivial subtorus of relative dimension 1.

(iii) There exists a homomorphism of groups \(\mathbf{G}_{a,\,S} \to G\) which is a closed immersion.

Then one has (i) \(\Leftrightarrow\) (ii) \(\Leftrightarrow\) (ii bis) \(\Rightarrow\) (iii).

The only new assertion is (i) \(\Rightarrow\) (iii). So let \(P\) be a parabolic subgroup of \(G\), distinct from \(G\). Then \(U = \mathrm{rad}^u(P) \neq e\). Consider the last non-trivial subgroup \(U_n\) of the composition series of \(U\) (2.1). One has an isomorphism \(U_n \simeq \mathbf{W}(\mathscr{E}_n)\), where \(\mathscr{E}_n\) is a locally free, hence free, \(\mathscr{O}_S\)-Module. Since \(\mathscr{E}_n \neq 0\), there exists a monomorphism \(\mathscr{O}_S \to \mathscr{E}_n\) which is locally a direct summand, hence a closed immersion \(\mathbf{G}_{a,\,S} = \mathbf{W}(\mathscr{O}_S) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{W}(\mathscr{E}_n) \simeq U_n\), which entails (iii) at once.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 6.12.1

When \(S\) is the spectrum of a field of characteristic 0, it follows from the Jacobson-Morozov theorem that (iii) \(\Rightarrow\) (ii bis). The four preceding conditions are then equivalent ("Godement's criterion", cf. [BT], 8.5). (*)
(*) This is more generally true when \(S\) is the spectrum of a perfect field (TITS).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 6.13

Let \(S\) be a connected semi-local scheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group. One says that \(G\) is anisotropic if \(G\) contains no trivial subtorus other than \(e\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.14

For the reductive \(S\)-group \(G\) to be anisotropic, it is necessary and sufficient that it possess no parabolic subgroup \(P \neq G\), and that its radical be anisotropic.
Using now 6.6, Exp. XXIV, 4.1.5, and Exp. XXII, 6.2, one deduces from this:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.15

Let \(S\) be a connected semi-local scheme, \(G\) an isotrivial reductive \(S\)-group (for example \(G\) semi-simple, or \(S\) normal). For \(G\) to be anisotropic, it is necessary and sufficient that \(G\) possess no parabolic subgroup \(P \neq G\), and that \(\mathrm{Hom}_{S\text{-gr.}}(G, \mathbf{G}_{m,\,S}) = e\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.16

Let \(S\) be a connected semi-local scheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group. The maximal trivial subtori of \(G\) are the largest trivial central subtori of the Levi groups of the minimal parabolic subgroups of \(G\). Two such tori are conjugate by an element of \(G(S)\).

Let \(Q\) be a maximal trivial subtorus of \(G\). Then \(Q = \mathrm{rad}(\underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q))_{\text{dép}}\), and (6.2), \(L = \underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q)\) is a Levi subgroup of a parabolic subgroup \(P\) of \(G\). By 6.11, \(L\) is a minimal element of the set of Levi subgroups of parabolic subgroups of \(G\), hence \(P\) is a minimal parabolic subgroup of \(G\) by 1.20. It then follows from 5.7 and 5.5 (iv) that two tori such as \(Q\) are conjugate by a section of \(G(S)\). The conjugacy of the \(Q\)'s and of the pairs \((P, L)\) then entails the first assertion of 6.16.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.17

Let \(S\) be a connected semi-local scheme, \(P\) and \(P'\) two minimal parabolic subgroups in standard position (4.5.1). Then \(P \cap P'\) contains a Levi subgroup common to \(P\) and \(P'\).

Indeed, \(P \cap P'\) contains a maximal torus \(T\) of \(G\), by 4.5.1; let \(L\) be the unique Levi subgroup of \(P\) containing \(T\). One has \[ \mathrm{rad}(P) \cap T = \mathrm{rad}(P) \cap L = \mathrm{rad}(L) \] by 1.21, hence \(\mathrm{rad}(P) \cap T\) contains \(\mathrm{rad}(L)_{\text{dép}}\), which is a maximal trivial subtorus of \(G\), and hence is necessarily equal to \(T_{\text{dép}}\). One therefore has \(L = \underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(T_{\text{dép}})\), and by symmetry \(L\) is also a Levi subgroup of \(P'\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 6.18

It follows from 1.21 that the parabolic subgroup \(P\) of \(G\) is minimal if and only if \(\mathrm{rad}(P)\) contains a maximal trivial subtorus of \(G\); then, by 6.17, if \(T\) is a maximal torus of \(P\), \(T_{\text{dép}}\) is a maximal torus of \(G\) and of \(\mathrm{rad}(P)\) and \(\underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(T_{\text{dép}})\) is a Levi subgroup of \(P\). Moreover, every Levi subgroup of \(P\) is obtained in this way.
7. Relative root datum

In this section, \(S\) will denote a non-empty connected semi-local scheme, \(G\) a reductive \(S\)-group, \(Q\) a maximal trivial subtorus of \(G\), and \(L\) the centralizer of \(Q\) in \(G\), i.e. \(L = \underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q)\).

Since \(Q\) is the largest split central subtorus of \(L\), every section of \(G(S)\) which normalizes \(L\) normalizes \(Q\). One therefore has (cf. 7.1.1) \[ \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(L)(S) = \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(Q)(S). \]

On the other hand, we saw in 6.4 that the map \(G(S) \to (G/L)(S)\) is surjective. It follows that one has a canonical identification \[ \mathrm{W}_G(Q)(S) = (\underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(Q)/\underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q))(S) \simeq \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(L)(S)/L(S). \]

We shall denote by \(M\) the group \(\mathrm{Hom}_{S\text{-gr.}}(Q, \mathbf{G}_{m,\,S})\), so that one has a canonical isomorphism \(Q \simeq \mathrm{D}_S(M)\). We shall denote by \(\mathrm{W}\) the group of automorphisms of \(M\) defined by \(\mathrm{W}_G(Q)(S)\). One therefore has isomorphisms \[ \mathrm{W} \simeq \mathrm{W}_G(Q)(S) \simeq \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(L)(S)/L(S). \]

One does not have in general \(\underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(L) = \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(Q)\). Take for example for \(S\) the spectrum of a field \(k\) possessing a quadratic extension \(k'\), and for \(G\) the unitary group \(\text{Q-Ép}_{k'/k}(\mathrm{A}_2)\) (cf. Exp. XXIV, 3.11.2).
Since the minimal parabolic subgroups of \(G\) are its Borel groups, their Levi groups are maximal tori, and one has \((\underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(L)/L)(\overline{k}) = \mathfrak{S}_3\).

On the other hand, since \(G\) is not split, the maximal trivial tori of \(G\) are of dimension \(\leqslant 1\), hence isomorphic to \(\mathbf{G}_{m,\,k}\). Since \(\underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(Q)/L\) acts faithfully on \(Q\), one has \((\underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(Q)/Q)(\overline{k}) = \mathbf{Z}/2\mathbf{Z}\).

If \(P\) is a parabolic subgroup of \(G\) with Levi group \(L\) (such exist by 6.2), \(P\) is necessarily minimal (cf. 6.18). By the conjugacy of the minimal parabolic subgroups of \(G\) (5.7), the conjugacy of the Levi subgroups of a parabolic subgroup (1.8), and the relations \(P = \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(P)\), \(\underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(L) \cap P = L\) (1.6), the set of (minimal) parabolic subgroups of \(G\) with Levi group \(L\) is principal homogeneous under the group \(\mathrm{W}\).

The Lie Algebra of \(G\) decomposes under the action of \(Q\) as \[ \mathrm{Lie}(G) = \mathrm{Lie}(L) + \coprod_{\alpha \in R} \mathrm{Lie}(G)^\alpha, \] where \(R\) is the set of non-zero characters of \(Q\) such that \(\mathrm{Lie}(G)^\alpha \neq 0\) (roots of \(G\) relatively to \(Q\)).

Let us denote by \(M^*\) the group \(\mathrm{Hom}_{S\text{-gr.}}(\mathbf{G}_{m,\,S}, Q)\), which is in duality with \(M\) and on which \(\mathrm{W}\) acts in a natural manner by transport of structure.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 7.4

With the notations of 7.3, there exists a unique map \(\alpha \mapsto \alpha^*\) from \(R\) to \(M^*\) which defines in \((M, M^*)\) a root datum (Exp. XXI, 1.1) whose Weyl group is \(\mathrm{W}\).

Moreover, the parabolic subgroups \(P\) of \(G\) with Levi group \(L\) and the systems of positive roots \(R_+\) of \(R\) correspond bijectively under the relation \[ \mathrm{Lie}(P) = \mathrm{Lie}(L) \oplus \coprod_{\alpha \in R_+} \mathrm{Lie}(G)^\alpha. \]

Let us suppose first that the existence of the required map \(\alpha \mapsto \alpha^*\) has been proved. By Exp. XXI, 3.4.10, \(s_\alpha\) is the unique element of \(\mathrm{W}\) such that for every \(m \in M\), \(s_\alpha(m) - m\) is a rational multiple of \(\alpha\), which shows that \(s_\alpha\) is determined by \(\alpha\); since one then has \(\alpha^*(m) = m - s_\alpha(m)\), one sees that \(\alpha^*\) is determined by \(\alpha\), which proves the uniqueness of the map \(\alpha \mapsto \alpha^*\).

Let \(\alpha \in R\) and let \(\mathrm{L}_\alpha\) (resp. \(\mathrm{H}_\alpha\), resp. \(\mathrm{H}_{-\alpha}\)) be the unique smooth subgroup of \(G\) with connected fibres containing \(L\) and such that \[ \mathrm{Lie}(\mathrm{L}_\alpha) = \mathrm{Lie}(L) \oplus \coprod_{\gamma \in (\mathbf{Z}\alpha) \cap R} \mathrm{Lie}(G)^\gamma \] (resp. \[ \mathrm{Lie}(\mathrm{H}_\alpha) = \mathrm{Lie}(L) \oplus \coprod_{\gamma \in (\mathbf{N}\alpha) \cap R} \mathrm{Lie}(G)^\gamma, \] resp. \[ \mathrm{Lie}(\mathrm{H}_{-\alpha}) = \mathrm{Lie}(L) \oplus \coprod_{\gamma \in (\mathbf{N}(-\alpha)) \cap R} \mathrm{Lie}(G)^\gamma), \] (6.1): \(\mathrm{L}_\alpha\) is a reductive subgroup of \(G\), \(\mathrm{H}_\alpha\) and \(\mathrm{H}_{-\alpha}\) are parabolic subgroups of it with Levi group \(L\), and \(\mathrm{H}_\alpha\) and \(\mathrm{H}_{-\alpha}\) are opposite relatively to \(L\) (cf. 6.1 (ii)).

By 7.2, there exists therefore \(s_\alpha \in \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_{\mathrm{L}_\alpha}(Q)(S)/L(S) \in \mathrm{W}\) such that \(s_\alpha(\mathrm{H}_\alpha) = \mathrm{H}_{-\alpha}\). One has \(s_\alpha(\alpha) = -\alpha\) (for \(\alpha\) (resp. \(-\alpha\)) is the common divisor of the elements of \(R\) occurring in \(\mathrm{H}_\alpha\) (resp. \(\mathrm{H}_{-\alpha}\))), and one has \(s_\alpha^2 = \mathrm{id}\) (for \(s_\alpha^2(\mathrm{H}_\alpha)\) and \(\mathrm{H}_\alpha\) are both opposite to \(\mathrm{H}_{-\alpha}\) relatively to \(L\)). We have thus constructed an \(s_\alpha \in \mathrm{W}\) satisfying the following properties: \[ \mathrm{(x)} \qquad s_\alpha(\alpha) = -\alpha, \qquad s_\alpha^2 = \mathrm{id} \] \[ \mathrm{(xx)} \qquad s_\alpha \text{ can be represented by an element of } \mathrm{L}_\alpha(S). \] Let us moreover remark that \(s_\alpha\) is constructed in a canonical manner from \(\alpha\), and in particular that \[ \mathrm{(xxx)} \qquad \text{for every } w \in \mathrm{W} \text{, we have } w s_\alpha w^{-1} = s_{w(\alpha)}. \]

We now propose to prove the assertion: \[ \mathrm{(xxxx)} \qquad \text{for every } m \in M, \quad s_\alpha(m) - m \in \mathbf{Z}\alpha. \] Since \(S\) is connected, this assertion is local for the (fpqc) topology. We may therefore assume that \(\mathrm{L}_\alpha = G_1\) is splittable relatively to a maximal torus \(T_1\) of \(L\). So let \((G_1, T_1, M_1, R_1)\) be such a splitting. The monomorphism \(Q \to T_1\) identifies \(M\) with a quotient of \(M_1\); let \(p : M_1 \to M\) be the canonical map.

The image of \(R_1\) under \(p\) consists possibly of zero and of the roots of \(G_1\) with respect to \(Q\) (hence of the elements of \(R\) which are integral multiples of \(\alpha\)); one therefore has \(p(R_1) \subset \mathbf{Z}\alpha\). By (xx), there exists an element of \(\underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_{G_1}(L)(S)\) which induces \(s_\alpha\) on \(Q\). By Exp. XXII, 5.10.10, there exists therefore a section \(w \in (\mathrm{W}_1)_S(S)\) which induces \(s_\alpha\) on \(Q\) (we denote by \(\mathrm{W}_1\) the Weyl group of the root datum \((M_1, R_1, \ldots)\)). After possibly shrinking \(S\), we may therefore assume that there exists \(w \in \mathrm{W}_1\) inducing \(s_\alpha\) on \(Q\), hence satisfying \(p(w(m_1)) = s_\alpha(p(m_1))\) for every \(m_1 \in M_1\). But, by definition of \(\mathrm{W}_1\), \(w\) is a product of symmetries with respect to elements of \(R_1\), hence \(w(m_1) - m_1\) is a linear combination with integral coefficients of the elements of \(R_1\). It follows that \(s_\alpha(p(m_1)) - p(m_1)\) is a linear combination with integral coefficients of the elements of \(p(R_1) \subset \mathbf{Z}\alpha\), hence an integral multiple of \(\alpha\), which is what was to be proved.

One may therefore define an element \(\alpha^* \in M^*\) by \[ \alpha^*(m) = m - s_\alpha(m). \] By (x), one has \((\alpha^*, \alpha) = 2\); it follows on the other hand from (xxx) that for every pair \((\alpha, \alpha') \in R \times R\), one has \(s_\alpha(\alpha') \in R\) and \(s_\alpha(\alpha'^*) = s_\alpha(\alpha')^*\), which proves (cf. Exp. XXI, 1.1) that the map \(\alpha \mapsto \alpha^*\) constructed does indeed define a root datum in \((M, M^*)\).
Let \(\mathrm{W}'\) be the Weyl group of this root datum (the group of transformations of \(M\) generated by the \(s_\alpha\)); one has \(\mathrm{W}' \subset \mathrm{W}\).

On the other hand, let \(\geqslant\) be a total order relation on the group \(M\); set \(R_+ = \{\alpha \in R \mid \alpha \geqslant 0\}\). It is known that \(R_+\) is a system of positive roots of \(R\). Let \(w \in \mathrm{W}\), represented by an \(n \in \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(L)(S) = \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(Q)(S)\). Set \(P = \mathrm{H}_{R_+}\) (notation of 6.1); by loc. cit., \(P\) is a parabolic subgroup of \(G\), with Levi group \(L\). One evidently has \(\mathrm{int}(n)P = \mathrm{H}_{w(R_+)}\). It then follows from 7.3 that \(w(R_+) = R_+\) entails \(w = e\). Since the group \(\mathrm{W}'\) acts transitively on the systems of positive roots of \(R\) (Exp. XXI, 3.3.7) and since the stabilizer in \(\mathrm{W}\) of \(R_+\) is the identity, one concludes at once that \(\mathrm{W} = \mathrm{W}'\). One also concludes that \(\mathrm{W} = \mathrm{W}'\) acts simply transitively both on the set of systems of positive roots of \(R\) and on the set of parabolic subgroups of \(G\) with Levi group \(L\), which entails the last assertion of 7.4. Q.E.D.

If \(P\) and \(P_1\) are two minimal parabolic subgroups of \(G\), with Levi groups \(L\) and \(L_1\), and if we denote by \(Q\) and \(Q_1\) the maximal trivial central tori of \(L\) and \(L_1\), then the pairs \((P, Q)\) and \((P_1, Q_1)\) are conjugate: there exists \(g \in G(S)\) with \(\mathrm{int}(g)P = P_1\), \(\mathrm{int}(g)Q = Q_1\).

Indeed, \(P\) and \(P_1\) are conjugate (5.7) and one may therefore assume \(P = P_1\); then \(L\) and \(L_1\) are conjugate by a section of \(P(S)\) (1.8). Moreover, if \(g\) and \(g'\) are two sections of \(G\) conjugating the pairs \((P, Q)\) and \((P_1, Q_1)\), \(g'^{-1}g\) normalizes \(P\) and \(Q\), hence \(P\) and \(L\); but \[ \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(P) \cap \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(L) = P \cap \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(L) = L = \underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q). \] The isomorphism \(Q \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } Q_1\) induced by \(\mathrm{int}(g)\) is therefore independent of \(g\).

Let \(\mathscr{R}\) and \(\mathscr{R}_1\) be the root data defined by means of 7.4 in \(\mathrm{Hom}_{S\text{-gr.}}(Q, \mathbf{G}_{m,\,S})\) and \(\mathrm{Hom}_{S\text{-gr.}}(Q_1, \mathbf{G}_{m,\,S})\) and let \(R_+\) and \(R_{1+}\) be the systems of positive roots corresponding to \(P\) and \(P_1\). The canonical isomorphism \(Q \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } Q_1\) defined above transforms \((\mathscr{R}, R_+)\) into \((\mathscr{R}_1, R_{1+})\). One deduces at once that one may define the pinned relative root datum of \(G\) over \(S\), by identifying the various \((\mathscr{R}, R_+)\) by means of the transitive system of isomorphisms described above.

From now on, we shall denote this pinned root datum by \((\underline{M}, \underline{M}^*, \underline{R}, \underline{R}^*, \underline{R}_+) = \underline{\mathscr{R}} = \mathscr{R}(G/S)\); for each pair \((P, Q)\) as above, one thus has a canonical isomorphism \(\underline{M} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Hom}_{S\text{-gr.}}(Q, \mathbf{G}_{m,\,S})\) transforming \(\underline{R}\) into the set of roots of \(G\) relatively to \(Q\), \(\underline{R}_+\) into the set of roots of \(P\) relatively to \(Q\), and \(\mathrm{W}(\underline{\mathscr{R}})\) into \(\mathrm{W}_G(Q)(S)\).

Let \(Q\) still be a maximal trivial torus of \(G\), \(P\) a (minimal) parabolic subgroup of \(G\) with Levi group \(\underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q)\), \((M, M^*, R, R^*, R_+)\) the corresponding pinned root datum (7.4), \(R_0\) the set of simple roots of \(R_+\). For every \(A \subset R_0\), let \(R_A \subset R\) be the set \[ R_A = R_+ \cup (\mathbf{Z}A \cap R_-) \] consisting of the positive roots together with those negative roots that are linear combinations of the elements of \(A\). It is a closed set (Exp. XXI, 3.1.4) of roots, and every closed set containing \(R_+\) can be put in this form in a unique way (Exp. XXI, 3.3.10). By 6.1, there exists a unique subgroup \(P_A\) of \(G\), smooth and with connected fibres, containing \(\underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q)\) and such that \[ \mathrm{Lie}(P_A) = \mathrm{Lie}(G)^0 \oplus \coprod_{\alpha \in R_A} \mathrm{Lie}(G)^\alpha. \]

It then follows at once from 6.1, from the conjugacy of the minimal parabolics, and from the fact that the set of roots of a parabolic subgroup of \(G\) containing \(Q\) is closed (which follows at once from 1.4 by splitting) that:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 7.7

(i) The map \(A \mapsto P_A\) is a bijection from the set of subsets of \(R_0\) onto the set of parabolic subgroups of \(G\) containing \(P\). This bijection preserves the natural order relations of inclusion.

(ii) Every parabolic subgroup of \(G\) is conjugate, by a section of \(G(S)\), to a unique \(P_A\).

Let \((P, Q)\) be as above. Consider the relative root datum (7.5) of \(G\) over \(S\) and the canonical isomorphism \[ f : \quad (M, M^*, R, R^*, R_+) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } (\underline{M}, \underline{M}^*, \underline{R}, \underline{R}^*, \underline{R}_+). \] The set \(R_0\) of simple roots of \(R_+\) is carried onto the set \(\underline{R}_0\) of simple roots of \(\underline{R}_+\), hence every subset \(A\) of \(R_0\) onto a subset \(f(A) \subset \underline{R}_0\).

Let \(H\) be an arbitrary parabolic subgroup of \(G\). By 7.7 (ii), it is conjugate to a unique \(P_A\). Let us write \(\mathbf{t}_\alpha(H) = f(A) \subset \underline{R}_0\). One checks at once, using the conjugacy theorems, that \(\mathbf{t}_\alpha(H)\) is independent of the choice of the couple \((P, Q)\). It is called the relative type of \(H\), and one has the

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 7.9

(i) The map \(H \mapsto \mathbf{t}_{\mathrm{r}}(H)\) induces a bijection between the set of conjugacy classes (under \(G(S)\)) of parabolic subgroups of \(G\), and the set of subsets of \(\underline{R}_0\).

(ii) Let \(H\) be a parabolic subgroup of \(G\), \(P\) a minimal parabolic subgroup contained in \(H\), \(Q\) the maximal central trivial torus of a Levi subgroup of \(P\), \(R_0\) the set of simple roots of \(P\) relative to \(Q\), and \(f : R_0 \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \underline{R}_0\) the canonical isomorphism. Then \[ f(r) \in \mathbf{t}_{\mathrm{r}}(H) \Longleftrightarrow \mathrm{Lie}(H)^{-\alpha} \neq 0 \] and one has \(H = P_A\), where \(A = f^{-1}(\mathbf{t}_{\mathrm{r}}(H))\).

(iii) If \(H\) and \(H'\) are two parabolic subgroups of \(G\) containing \(P\), then (see 3.8.1 (ii) and 5.5 (i) for other equivalent conditions): \[ \mathbf{t}_{\mathrm{r}}(H) \subset \mathbf{t}_{\mathrm{r}}(H') \Longleftrightarrow \mathbf{t}(H) \subset \mathbf{t}(H') \]
One can study the relative positions of two minimal parabolic subgroups; the results are the following:

(1) If \(P\), \(P_1\), \(P'\), \(P'_1\) are four minimal parabolic subgroups of \(G\), then \(\mathbf{t}_2(P, P_1) = \mathbf{t}_2(P', P'_1)\) (cf. 4.5.2) i.e. \((P, P_1)\) and \((P', P'_1)\) are conjugate locally for (fpqc)) if and only if there exists \(g \in G(S)\) with \(\mathrm{int}(g)P = P'\), \(\mathrm{int}(g)P_1 = P'_1\).

(2) Let us fix in particular a minimal parabolic subgroup \(P\) with Levi group \(L\) and let \(T\) be a maximal torus of \(L\). Consider the scheme \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}_{t_{\min}}(G; P)\) of minimal parabolic subgroups of \(G\) in standard position relative to \(P\). One has a morphism (cf. 4.5.5) \[ f : \underline{\mathrm{Par}}_{t_{\min}}(G; P) \longrightarrow \mathrm{W}_P(T) \backslash \mathrm{W}_G(T) / \mathrm{W}_P(T) \] whose fibres are "the orbits of \(P\) in \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}_{t_{\min}}(G; P)\)". By (1), \(f\) therefore induces a monomorphism \[ P(S) \backslash \underline{\mathrm{Par}}_{t_{\min}}(G; P)(S) \hookrightarrow \big(\mathrm{W}_P(T) \backslash \mathrm{W}_G(T) / \mathrm{W}_P(T)\big)(S). \]

The image of this morphism is identified with \(\mathrm{W}\); this is the Bruhat theorem: each orbit of \(P(S)\) in \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}_{t_{\min}}(G; P)(S)\) contains one and only one parabolic subgroup of \(G\) with Levi group \(L\) (that is to say, of the form \(\mathrm{int}(n)P\), where \(n \in \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(L)\)).

(3) In other words, let \(E\) be the set of \(g \in G(S)\) such that \(\mathrm{int}(g)P\) and \(P\) are in standard mutual position. Then \(E\) admits a partition into double cosets modulo \(P(S)\) indexed by \(\mathrm{W}\): \[ E = P(S)\, \mathrm{W}\, P(S) \qquad \text{(obvious notation)}. \] One may also write, with \(U = \mathrm{rad}^u(P)(S)\), \[ E = U(S) \cdot \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(L)(S) \cdot U(S), \] thus exhibiting a partition of \(E\) into double cosets modulo \(U(S)\), indexed by \(\underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(L)(S)\).
(4) If \(S\) is the spectrum of a field, then \(E = G(S)\), and one recovers [BT], 5.15.

blocks.title: Counterexamples
blocks.html:
Counterexamples 7.11

Let \(S = \mathrm{Spec}(\mathbf{Z}/4\mathbf{Z})\), \(G = \mathrm{SL}_{2,\,S}\). Let \(B\) be the usual Borel group consisting of the matrices \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{smallmatrix}\right)\) with \(c = 0\). Let \(g = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \end{smallmatrix}\right) \in G(S)\), and set \(B' = \mathrm{int}(g)B\). Then \(B(S) = B'(S)\), and \(B \cap B'\) contains no maximal torus. This shows on the one hand that two distinct minimal parabolic subgroups may have the same group of sections, and on the other hand that there exists in general no criterion allowing one to recognise whether two minimal parabolic subgroups \(P\) and \(P'\) are in standard position, by means of the groups \(P(S)\) and \(P'(S)\) alone. In particular, the subset \(E\) of \(G(S)\) does not seem to be definable by means of the situation \(\{G(S), P(S), \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(L)(S)\}\) alone (in the preceding case, this subset is defined by \(c \neq 2\)).

We now propose to study the variation of \(\mathscr{R}(G/S)\) with \(S\). Let then \(S'\) be an \(S\)-scheme, likewise semi-local, connected and non-empty. Let \(Q\) be a maximal trivial torus of \(G\); then \(Q_{S'}\) is a trivial torus of \(G_{S'}\); let \(Q'\) be a maximal trivial torus of \(G_{S'}\) containing \(Q_{S'}\). Set \[ \begin{aligned} M &= \mathrm{Hom}_{S\text{-gr.}}(Q, \mathbf{G}_{m,\,S}) \simeq \mathrm{Hom}_{S'\text{-gr.}}(Q_{S'}, \mathbf{G}_{m,\,S'}) \\ M' &= \mathrm{Hom}_{S'\text{-gr.}}(Q', \mathbf{G}_{m,\,S'}). \end{aligned} \]

The monomorphism \(Q_{S'} \to Q'\) induces an epimorphism \(u : M' \to M\). Let us write \[ L = \underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q), \qquad L' = \underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_{G_{S'}}(Q'), \] one has \(L' \subset L_{S'}\).

If \(H\) is a subgroup of \(G\) containing \(L\), then \(H_{S'}\) contains \(L'\), and one has \[ \mathrm{Lie}(H) = \mathrm{Lie}(L) \oplus \coprod_{\alpha \in R} \mathrm{Lie}(H)^\alpha \] \[ \mathrm{Lie}(H_{S'}) = \mathrm{Lie}(L') \oplus \coprod_{\alpha' \in R'} \mathrm{Lie}(H_{S'})^{\alpha'}, \] where \(R_H\) (resp. \(R'_{H_{S'}}\)) denotes the set of roots of \(H\) (resp. \(H_{S'}\)) relative to \(Q\) (resp. \(Q'\)). One deduces immediately that \[ R_H \subset u(R'_{H_{S'}}) \subset R_H \cup \{0\}. \]

Taking \(H = G\), one sees first that \(R \subset u(R') \subset R \cup \{0\}\); then taking for \(H\) a minimal parabolic subgroup \(P\) with Levi group \(L\), one sees that \(R'_{H_{S'}}\) contains a system of positive roots of \(R'\), hence (7.4) that there exists a minimal parabolic subgroup \(P'\) of \(G_{S'}\) with Levi group \(L'\) contained in \(P_{S'}\). We have thus constructed a diagram \[ \begin{array}{ccccc} Q_{S'} & \subset & L_{S'} & \subset & P_{S'} \\ \cap & & \cup & & \cup \\ Q' & \subset & L' & \subset & P'. \end{array} \]

If \(R_+\) (resp. \(R_0\)) is the system of positive (resp. simple) roots of \(R\) defined by \(P\), and if one defines \(R'_+\) and \(R'_0\) in the same way, one checks easily that \(R_+ \subset u(R'_+) \subset R_+ \cup \{0\}\), and that \(R_0 \subset u(R'_0) \subset R_0 \cup \{0\}\).

Let now \(w \in \mathrm{W} \simeq \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(Q)(S)/\underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_G(Q)(S)\), represented by \(n \in \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_G(Q)(S)\). One has \(\mathrm{int}(n)Q = Q\), hence \(\mathrm{int}(n)L = L\), hence \(\mathrm{int}(n)L_{S'} = L_{S'}\). Then \(Q'\) and \(\mathrm{int}(n)Q'\) are two maximal trivial tori of \(L_{S'}\), hence are conjugate by a section \(x \in L(S')\), and one has \(\mathrm{int}(nx)Q' = Q'\), hence \(nx \in \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_{G_{S'}}(Q')(S')\). Let \(w'\) be the image of \(n' = nx\) in \(\mathrm{W}' \simeq \underline{\mathrm{Norm}}_{G_{S'}}(Q')(S')/\underline{\mathrm{Centr}}_{G_{S'}}(Q')(S')\). It is clear that the action of \(w'\) on \(M'\) is compatible with the projection \(u : M' \to M\) and that the induced action on \(M\) coincides with that defined by \(w\).
Using now the definition of the relative root data and the conjugacy theorems, one proves without difficulty:

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 7.13

Let \(S\) and \(S'\) be two non-empty connected semi-local schemes, \(S' \to S\) a morphism of \(S\)-preschemes, \(G\) an \(S\)-reductive group, \[ \mathscr{R}(G/S) = (\underline{M}, \underline{M}^*, \underline{R}, \underline{R}^*, \underline{R}_+), \qquad \mathscr{R}(G_{S'}/S') = (\underline{M}', \underline{M}'^*, \underline{R}', \underline{R}'^*, \underline{R}'_+) \] the relative pinned root data. There exists a canonical homomorphism \[ \underline{u} : \underline{M}' \longrightarrow \underline{M} \] satisfying the following conditions:

(i) \(\underline{u}\) is surjective.

(ii) For every \(w \in \mathrm{W}\), there exists an element \(w'\) of \(\mathrm{W}'\) compatible with \(\underline{u}\) and inducing \(w\) on \(\underline{M}\).

(iii) For every subset \(X\) of \(\underline{M}\), let us write \(X^\wedge = X \cap (\underline{M} - \{0\})\). Then \[ \underline{u}(\underline{R}'_+)^\wedge = \underline{R}_+, \qquad \underline{u}(\underline{R}'_0)^\wedge = \underline{R}_0. \]

(iv) For every parabolic subgroup \(H\) of \(G\) consider \(\mathbf{t}_{\mathrm{r}}(H) \subset \underline{R}_0\) and \(\mathbf{t}_{\mathrm{r}}(H_{S'}) \subset \underline{R}'_0\). Then \[ \mathbf{t}_{\mathrm{r}}(H_{S'}) = \underline{u}^{-1}\big(\mathbf{t}_{\mathrm{r}}(H) \cup \{0\}\big) \cap \underline{R}'_0 = \{\alpha' \in \underline{R}'_0 \mid \underline{u}(\alpha') \in \mathbf{t}_{\mathrm{r}}(H) \text{ or } \underline{u}(\alpha') = 0\}. \]

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 7.14

If \(G\) is splittable over \(S\), its maximal trivial tori are maximal tori, and the relative notions introduced here then coincide with the absolute notations already introduced. The preceding theorem thus gives a description of the relative root datum \(\mathscr{R}(G/S)\) and of the relative type \(\mathbf{t}_{\mathrm{r}}\), by means of the absolute root datum and the absolute type of the group \(G_{S'}\), \(S'\) being chosen in such a way that \(G_{S'}\) be splittable (cf. Exp. XXIV, 4.4.1). We refer to [BT], 6.12 et seq. for this description.

Let \(S\) be a henselian local scheme, \(s\) its closed point, \(S_0\) the spectrum of the residue field of \(s_0\), identified with a closed subscheme of \(S\); for every object \(X\) over \(S\), let us write \(X_0\) for the object over \(S_0\) deduced from \(X\) by base change. Finally, let \(G\) be an \(S\)-reductive group. For every parabolic subgroup \(P\) of \(G\), \(P_0\) is a parabolic subgroup of \(G_0\); conversely, for every parabolic subgroup \(\overline{P}\) of \(G_0\), there exists a parabolic subgroup \(P\) of \(G\) such that \(P_0 = \overline{P}\) (this follows from Hensel's lemma and from the fact that \(\underline{\mathrm{Par}}(G)\) is a smooth \(S\)-scheme); in particular (confer 5.7), a parabolic subgroup \(P\) of \(G\) is minimal if and only if \(P_0\) is minimal. Such a subgroup \(P\) of \(G\) being chosen, an analogous argument shows that the maximal trivial subtori of \(P_0\) are of the form \(T_0\), where \(T\) is a maximal trivial subtorus of \(P\). It follows without difficulty that the relative root data of \(G\) over \(S\) and of \(G_0\) over \(S_0\) are canonically isomorphic, so that the theory of the parabolic subgroups of \(G\) reduces to that of the parabolic subgroups of \(G_0\).

Let us remark moreover that every \(S_0\)-reductive group is of the form \(G_0\) (Exp. XXIV, Prop. 1.21), which conversely makes it possible to reduce the study of the parabolic subgroups of an \(S_0\)-reductive group to the corresponding study over \(S\).
